**Compatible release requirements** specify a minimal version with the ability to update to later versions of the same level.
For example, if you specify a major, minor, and patch version, only patch-level changes are allowed.
If you only specify a major, and minor version, then minor- and patch-level changes are allowed.
`~=1.2.3` is an example of a compatible release requirement.
**Wildcard requirements** allow for the latest (dependency-dependent) version where the wildcard is positioned.
`*`, `1.*` and `1.2.*` are examples of wildcard requirements.
**Inequality requirements** allow manually specifying a version range or an exact version to depend on.
Here are some examples of inequality requirements:
Multiple version requirements can also be separated with a comma, e.g. `>= 1.2, < 1.5`.
You can specify the exact version of a package.
`1.2.3` is an example of an exact version specification.
This will tell Poetry to install this version and this version only.
If other dependencies require a different version, the solver will ultimately fail and abort any installation or update procedures.
Exact versions can also be specified with `==` according to [PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/).
When using `poetry add` such constraints are automatically converted into an equivalent constraint.

**Caret requirements** allow [SemVer](https://semver.org/) compatible updates to a specified version. An update is allowed if the new version number does not modify the left-most non-zero digit in the major, minor, patch grouping. For instance, if we previously ran `poetry add requests@^2.13.0` and wanted to update the library and ran `poetry update requests`, poetry would update us to version `2.14.0` if it was available, but would not update us to `3.0.0`. If instead, we had specified the version string as `^0.1.13`, poetry would update to `0.1.14` but not `0.2.0`. `0.0.x` is not considered compatible with any other version.
Here are some more examples of caret requirements and the versions that would be allowed with them:
When using `poetry add` such constraints are automatically converted into an equivalent constraint.
**Tilde requirements** specify a minimal version with some ability to update.
If you specify a major, minor, and patch version or only a major and minor version, only patch-level changes are allowed.
If you only specify a major version, then minor- and patch-level changes are allowed.
`~1.2.3` is an example of a tilde requirement.

### Why is the dependency resolution process slow?
While the dependency resolver at the heart of Poetry is highly optimized and
should be fast enough for most cases, with certain sets of dependencies,
it can take time to find a valid solution.
This is due to the fact that not all libraries on PyPI have properly declared their metadata
and, as such, they are not available via the PyPI JSON API. At this point, Poetry has no choice
but to download the packages and inspect them to get the necessary information. This is an expensive
operation, both in bandwidth and time, which is why it seems this is a long process.
At the moment, there is no way around it. However, if you notice that Poetry
is downloading many versions of a single package, you can lessen the workload
by constraining that one package in your pyproject.toml more narrowly. That way,
Poetry does not have to sift through so many versions of it, which may speed up
the locking process considerably in some cases.

### What kind of versioning scheme does Poetry use for itself?
Poetry uses "major.minor.micro" version identifiers as mentioned in
Version bumps are done similar to Python's versioning:
* A major version bump (incrementing the first number) is only done for breaking changes
if a deprecation cycle is not possible, and many users have to perform some manual steps
to migrate from one version to the next one.
* A minor version bump (incrementing the second number) may include new features as well
as new deprecations and drop features deprecated in an earlier minor release.
* A micro version bump (incrementing the third number) usually only includes bug fixes.
Deprecated features will not be dropped in a micro release.
### Why does Poetry not adhere to semantic versioning?
Because of its large user base, even small changes not considered relevant by most users
can turn out to be a breaking change for some users in hindsight.
Sticking to strict [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) and (almost) always bumping
the major version instead of the minor version does not seem desirable
since the minor version will not carry any meaning anymore.
### Are unbound version constraints a bad idea?
A version constraint without an upper bound such as `*` or `>=3.4` will allow updates to any future version of the dependency.
This includes major versions breaking backward compatibility.
Once a release of your package is published, you cannot tweak its dependencies anymore in case a dependency breaks BC
– you have to do a new release but the previous one stays broken.
(Users can still work around the broken dependency by restricting it by themselves.)
To avoid such issues, you can define an upper bound on your constraints,
which you can increase in a new release after testing that your package is compatible
with the new major version of your dependency.
For example, instead of using `>=3.4` you can use `^3.4` which allows all versions `<4.0`.
The `^` operator works very well with libraries following [semantic versioning](https://semver.org).
However, when defining an upper bound, users of your package are not able to update
a dependency beyond the upper bound even if it does not break anything
and is fully compatible with your package.
You have to release a new version of your package with an increased upper-bound first.
If your package is used as a library in other packages, it might be better to avoid
upper bounds and thus unnecessary dependency conflicts (unless you already know for sure
that the next release of the dependency will break your package).
If your package is used as an application, it might be worth defining an upper bound.

### Why is Poetry telling me that the current project's supported Python range is not compatible with one or more packages' Python requirements?
Unlike `pip`, Poetry doesn't resolve for just the Python in the current environment. Instead, it makes sure that a dependency
is resolvable within the given Python version range in `pyproject.toml`.
This means your project aims to be compatible with any Python version >=3.7,<4.0. Whenever you try to add a dependency
whose Python requirement doesn't match the whole range, Poetry will tell you this, e.g.:
The current project's supported Python range (>=3.7.0,<4.0.0) is not compatible with some of the required packages Python requirement:
- scipy requires Python >=3.7,<3.11, so it will not be installable for Python >=3.11,<4.0.0
Usually you will want to match the supported Python range of your project with the upper bound of the failing dependency.
Alternatively, you can tell Poetry to install this dependency [only for a specific range of Python versions]({{< relref "dependency-specification#multiple-constraints-dependencies" >}}),
if you know that it's not needed in all versions.

This is done to be compliant with the broader Python ecosystem.

### Poetry busts my Docker cache because it requires me to COPY my source files in before installing 3rd party dependencies
By default, running `poetry install ...` requires you to have your source files present (both the "root" package and any directory path dependencies you might have).
This interacts poorly with Docker's caching mechanisms because any change to a source file will make any layers (subsequent commands in your Dockerfile) re-run.
For example, you might have a Dockerfile that looks something like this:
RUN pip install poetry && poetry install --only main

As soon as *any* source file changes, the cache for the `RUN` layer will be invalidated, which forces all 3rd party dependencies (likely the slowest step out of these) to be installed again if you changed any files in `src/`.
To avoid this cache busting you can split this into two steps:
2. Copy over your source code and install just the source code.
This might look something like this:
RUN pip install poetry && poetry install --only main --no-root --no-directory

The two key options we are using here are `--no-root` (skips installing the project source) and `--no-directory` (skips installing any local directory path dependencies, you can omit this if you don't have any).
[More information on the options available for `poetry install`]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}).

To install the defined dependencies for your project, just run the [`install`]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}) command.
When you run this command, one of two things may happen:
If you have never run the command before and there is also no `poetry.lock` file present,
Poetry simply resolves all dependencies listed in your `pyproject.toml` file and downloads the latest version of their files.
When Poetry has finished installing, it writes all the packages and their exact versions that it downloaded to the `poetry.lock` file,
locking the project to those specific versions.
You should commit the `poetry.lock` file to your project repo so that all people working on the project are locked to the same versions of dependencies (more below).
This brings us to the second scenario. If there is already a `poetry.lock` file as well as a `pyproject.toml` file
when you run `poetry install`, it means either you ran the `install` command before,
or someone else on the project ran the `install` command and committed the `poetry.lock` file to the project (which is good).
Either way, running `install` when a `poetry.lock` file is present resolves and installs all dependencies that you listed in `pyproject.toml`,
but Poetry uses the exact versions listed in `poetry.lock` to ensure that the package versions are consistent for everyone working on your project.
As a result you will have all dependencies requested by your `pyproject.toml` file,
but they may not all be at the very latest available versions
(some dependencies listed in the `poetry.lock` file may have released newer versions since the file was created).
This is by design, it ensures that your project does not break because of unexpected changes in dependencies.
### Committing your `poetry.lock` file to version control
Application developers commit `poetry.lock` to get more reproducible builds.
Committing this file to VC is important because it will cause anyone who sets up the project
to use the exact same versions of the dependencies that you are using.
Your CI server, production machines, other developers in your team,
everything and everyone runs on the same dependencies,
which mitigates the potential for bugs affecting only some parts of the deployments.
Even if you develop alone, in six months when reinstalling the project you can feel confident
the dependencies installed are still working even if your dependencies released many new versions since then.
(See note below about using the update command.)

{{% warning %}} If you have added the recommended [`[build-system]`]({{< relref "pyproject#poetry-and-pep-517" >}}) section to your project's pyproject.toml then you _can_ successfully install your project and its dependencies into a virtual environment using a command like `pip install -e .`. However, pip will not use the lock file to determine dependency versions as the poetry-core build system is intended for library developers (see next section).
Library developers have more to consider. Your users are application developers, and your library will run in a Python environment you don't control.

The application ignores your library's lock file. It can use whatever dependency version meets the constraints in your `pyproject.toml`. The application will probably use the latest compatible dependency version. If your library's `poetry.lock` falls behind some new dependency version that breaks things for your users, you're likely to be the last to find out about it.

A simple way to avoid such a scenario is to omit the `poetry.lock` file. However, by doing so, you sacrifice reproducibility and performance to a certain extent. Without a lockfile, it can be difficult to find the reason for failing tests, because in addition to obvious code changes an unnoticed library update might be the culprit. Further, Poetry will have to lock before installing a dependency if `poetry.lock` has been omitted. Depending on the number of dependencies, locking may take a significant amount of time.
If you do not want to give up the reproducibility and performance benefits, consider a regular refresh of `poetry.lock` to stay up-to-date and reduce the risk of sudden breakage for users.

* **Check the [FAQ]** for a list of common questions and problems.
* **Check the [blog]** for release notes from recent releases, including steps for upgrading and known issues.
* **Check that your issue does not already exist** in the [issue tracker].
* **Make sure your issue is really a bug, and is not a support request or question** better suited for [Discussions]
* **Try clearing your cache with** `poetry cache clear --all PyPI` **and rerunning your commands**.
If you find a **Closed** issue that seems like it is the same thing that you're experiencing, open a new issue and
include a link to the original issue in the body of your new one.
#### How do I submit a bug report?
Bugs concerning Poetry and poetry-core should be submitted to the main [issue tracker], using the correct
Explain the problem and make it easy for others to search for and understand:
* **Use a clear and descriptive title** for the issue to identify the problem.
* **Describe the exact steps which reproduce the problem** in as many details as possible.
* **Describe the behavior you observed after following the steps** and point out how this is a bug.
* **Explain which behavior you expected to see instead and why.**
* **If the problem involves an unexpected error being raised**, execute the problematic command in **debug** mode
Provide detailed steps for reproduction of your issue:
* **Provide your pyproject.toml file** in a [Gist](https://gist.github.com), pastebin, or example repository after
removing potential private information like private package repositories or names.
* **Provide specific examples to demonstrate the steps to reproduce the issue**. This could be an example repository, a
sequence of steps run in a container, or just a pyproject.toml for very simple cases.
* **Are you unable to reliably reproduce the issue?** If so, provide details about how often the problem happens
and under which conditions it normally happens.
Provide more context by answering these questions:
* **Did the problem start happening recently** (e.g., after updating to a new version of Poetry) or was this always a
* If the problem started happening recently, **can you reproduce the problem in an older version of Poetry?** What's the
most recent version in which the problem does not happen?
* **Is there anything exotic or unusual about your environment?** This could include use of special container images,
newer CPU architectures like Apple Silicon, or corporate proxies that intercept or modify your network traffic.
Include details about your configuration and environment:
* **Which version of Poetry are you using?** You can get the exact version by running `poetry --version`.
* **What version of Python is being used to run Poetry?** Execute the `poetry debug info` to get this information.
* **What's the name and version of the OS you're using?** Examples include Ubuntu 22.04 or macOS 12.6.
To give others the best chance to understand and reproduce your issue, please be sure to put extra effort into your
reproduction steps. You can both rule out local configuration issues on your end, and ensure others can cleanly
reproduce your issue if attempt all reproductions in a pristine container (or VM), and provide the steps you performed
inside that container/VM in your issue report.

You must assume that only Python built-ins are available by default in a build environment. This means, if you need

### When is my build script executed?
If your project uses a build script, it is run implicitly in the following scenarios.
1. When `poetry install` is run, it is executed prior to installing the project's root package.
2. When `poetry build` is run, it is executed prior to building distributions.
3. When a PEP 517 build is triggered from source or sdist by another build frontend.
### How does Poetry ensure my build script's dependencies are met?
Prior to executing the build script, Poetry creates a temporary virtual environment with your project's active Python
version and then installs all dependencies specified under `build-system.requires` into this environment. It should be
noted that no packages will be present in this environment at the time of creation.

to make sure the poetry configuration does not get committed in a broken state.

The `poetry-lock` hook calls the `poetry lock` command
to make sure the lock file is up-to-date when committing changes.
The hook takes the same arguments as the poetry command.
For more information see the [lock command]({{< relref "cli#lock" >}}).
The `poetry-export` hook calls the `poetry export` command
to sync your `requirements.txt` file with your current dependencies.

[setting-valueN] 308|```` 309| 310|`setting-key` is a configuration option name and `setting-value1` is a configuration value. 311|See [Configuration]({{< relref "configuration" >}}) for all available settings. 312| 313|{{% warning %}} 314|Use `--` to terminate option parsing if your values may start with a hyphen (`-`), e.g. 315|```bash 316|poetry config http-basic.custom-repo gitlab-ci-token -- ${GITLAB_JOB_TOKEN} 317|``` 318|Without `--` this command will fail if `${GITLAB_JOB_TOKEN}` starts with a hyphen. 319|{{% /warning%}} 320| 321|#### Options 322| 323|* `--unset`: Remove the configuration element named by `setting-key`. 324|* `--list`: Show the list of current config variables. 325|* `--local`: Set/Get settings that are specific to a project (in the local configuration file `poetry.toml`). 326|* `--migrate`: Migrate outdated configuration settings. 327| 328|## debug 329| 330|The `debug` command groups subcommands that are useful for, as the name suggests, debugging issues you might have 331|when using Poetry with your projects. 332| 333|### debug info 334| 335|The `debug info` command shows debug information about Poetry and your project's virtual environment. 336| 337|### debug resolve 338| 339|The `debug resolve` command helps when debugging dependency resolution issues. optional. 17|In non-package mode, the `name` and `version` fields are required 18|if using the `project` section. 19| 20|{{% note %}} 21|Run `poetry check` to print warnings about deprecated fields. 22|{{% /note %}} 23| 24| 25|## The `project` section 26| 27|The `project` section of the `pyproject.toml` file according to the 28|[specification of the PyPA](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#declaring-project-metadata-the-project-table). 29| 30|### name 31| 32|The name of the package. **Always required when the `project` section is specified** 33| 34|This should be a valid name as defined by [PEP 508](https://peps.python.org/pep-0508/#names). 35| 36| 37|```toml 38|[project] 39|name = "my-package" 40|``` 41| 42|### version 43| 44|The version of the package. **Always required when the `project` section is specified** 45| 46|This should be a valid [PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/) string. 47| 48|```toml 49|[project] 50|# ... 51|version = "0.1.0" 52|``` 53| 54|If you want to set the version dynamically via `poetry build --local-version` 55|or you are using a plugin, which sets the version dynamically, you should add `version` 56|to dynamic and define the base version in the `tool.poetry` section, for example: 57| 58|```toml 59|[project] 60|name = "my-package" 61|dynamic = [ "version" ] 62| 63|[tool.poetry] 64|version = "1.0" # base version 65|``` 66| 67|### description 68| 69|A short description of the package. 70| 71|```toml 72|[project] 73|# ... 74|description = "A short description of the package." 75|``` 76| 77|### license 78| 79|An [SPDX expression](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/glossary/#term-License-Expression) 80|representing the license of the package. 81| 82|The recommended notation for the most common licenses is (alphabetical): 83| 84|* Apache-2.0 85|* BSD-2-Clause 86|* BSD-3-Clause 87|* BSD-4-Clause 88|* GPL-2.0-only 89|* GPL-2.0-or-later 90|* GPL-3.0-only 91|* GPL-3.0-or-later 92|* LGPL-2.1-only 93|* LGPL-2.1-or-later 94|* LGPL-3.0-only 95|* LGPL-3.0-or-later 96|* MIT 97| 98|Optional, but it is highly recommended to supply this. 99|More identifiers are listed at the [SPDX Open Source License Registry](https://spdx.org/licenses/). 100| 101|```toml 102|[project] 103|# ... 104|license = "MIT" 105|``` 106| 107|{{% warning %}} 108|Specifying license as a table, e.g. `{ text = "MIT" }` is deprecated. 109|If you used to specify a license file, e.g. `{ file = "LICENSE" }`, 110|use `license-files` instead. 111|{{% /warning %}} 112| 113|### license-files 114| 115|A list of glob patterns that match the license files of the package 116|relative to the root of the project source tree. 117| 118|```toml 119|[project] 120|# ... 121|license-files = [ 122| "*-LICENSE", 123| "CONTRIBUTORS", 124| "MY-SPECIAL-LICENSE-DIR/**/*" 125|] 126|``` 127| 128|By default, Poetry will include the following files: 129|- `LICENSE*` 130|- `LICENCE*` 131|- `COPYING*` 132|- `AUTHORS*` 133|- `NOTICE*` 134|- `LICENSES/**/*` 135| 136|{{% note %}} 137|The default applies only if the `license-files` field is not specified. 138|Specifying an empty list results in no license files being included. 139|{{% /note %}} 140| 141|### readme 142| 143|A path to the README file or the content. 144| 145|```toml 146|[project] 147|# ... 148|readme = "README.md" 149|``` 150| 151|{{% note %}} 152|If you want to define multiple README files, you have to add `readme` to `dynamic` 153|and define them in the `tool.poetry` section. 154|{{% /note %}} 155| 156|```toml 157|[project] 158|# ... 159|dynamic = [ "readme" ] 160| 161|[tool.poetry] 162|# ... 163|readme = ["docs/README1.md", "docs/README2.md"] 164|``` 165| 166|### requires-python 167| do not want to define an upper bound 178|in your package metadata, you can omit the upper bound in the `requires-python` field 179|and add it in the `tool.poetry.dependencies` section. 180|{{% /note entry maps a **command name** to a Python callable using 286|`package.module:function`. 317|Pass CLI arguments after the script name; parse them inside your function 318|(for example with [`argparse`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/argparse.html)). 319| 320|{{% note %}} 321|When a console script (entry point) is added or updated, run `poetry install` 322|again so the command wrappers are created/updated in the project's virtualenv. 323|This is the canonical place for that "#scripts-1" >}}) instead. 329|{{% /note %}} 330| 331|### gui-scripts 332| 333|This section describes the GUI scripts that will be installed when installing the package. 334| 335|```toml 4|type: docs 5|layout: single 6| 7|menu: 8| docs: 9| weight: 70 10|--- 11| 12|# Dependency specification 13| 14|Dependencies for a project can be specified in various forms, which depend on the type 15|of the dependency and on the optional constraints that might be needed for it to be installed. 16| 17|## `project.dependencies` and `tool.poetry.dependencies` 18| 19|Prior Poetry 2.0, dependencies had to be declared in the `tool.poetry.dependencies` 20|section of the `pyproject.toml` file. 21| 22|```toml 23|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 24|requests = "^2.13.0" 25|``` 26| 27|With Poetry 2.0, you should consider using the `project.dependencies` section instead. 28| 29|```toml 30|[project] 31|# ... 32|dependencies = [ 33| "requests (>=2.23.0,<3.0.0)" 34|] 35|``` 36| 37|While dependencies in `tool.poetry.dependencies` are specified using toml tables, 38|dependencies in `project.dependencies` are specified as strings according 39|to [PEP 508](https://peps.python.org/pep-0508/). 40| 41|In many cases, `tool.poetry.dependencies` can be replaced with `project.dependencies`. 42|However, there are some cases where you might still need to use `tool.poetry.dependencies`. 43|For example, if you want to define additional information that is not required for building 44|but only for locking (for example, an explicit source), you can enrich dependency 45|information in the `tool.poetry` section. 46| 47|```toml 48|[project] 49|# ... 50|dependencies = [ 51| "requests>=2.13.0", 52|] 53| 54|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 55|requests = { source = "private-source" } 56|``` 57| 58|When both are specified, `project.dependencies` are used for metadata when building the project, 59|`tool.poetry.dependencies` is only used to enrich `project.dependencies` for locking. 60| 61|Alternatively, you can add `dependencies` to `dynamic` and define your dependencies 62|completely in the `tool.poetry` section. Using only the `tool.poetry` section might 63|make sense in non-package mode when you will not build an sdist or a wheel. 64| 65|```toml 66|[project] 67|# ... 68|dynamic = [ "dependencies" ] 69| 70|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 71|requests = { version = ">=2.13.0", source = "private-source" } 72|``` 73| 74|{{% note %}} 75|Another use case for `tool.poetry.dependencies` are relative path dependencies 76|since `project.dependencies` only support absolute paths. 77|{{% /note %}} 78| 79|{{% note %}} 80|Only main dependencies can be specified in the `project` section. 81|Other [Dependency groups]({{< relref "managing-dependencies#dependency-groups" >}}) 82|must still be specified in the `tool.poetry` section. 83|{{% /note %}} 84| 85|## Version constraints 86| 87|### Compatible release requirements 88| 89|**Compatible release requirements** specify a minimal version with the ability to update to later versions of the same level. 90|For example, if you specify a major, minor, and patch version, only patch-level changes are allowed. 91|If you only specify a major, and minor version, then minor- and patch-level changes are allowed. 92| 93|`~=1.2.3` is an example of a compatible release requirement. 94| 95|| Requirement | Versions allowed | 96|| ----------- | ---------------- | 97|| ~=1.2.3 | >=1.2.3 <1.3.0 | 98|| ~=1.2 | >=1.2.0 <2.0.0 | 99| 100|### Wildcard requirements 101| 102|**Wildcard requirements** allow for the latest (dependency-dependent) version where the wildcard is positioned. 103| 104|`*`, `1.*` and `1.2.*` are examples of wildcard requirements. 105| 106|| Requirement | Versions allowed | 107|| ----------- | ---------------- | 108|| * | >=0.0.0 | 109|| 1.* | >=1.0.0 <2.0.0 | 110|| 1.2.* | >=1.2.0 <1.3.0 | 111| 112|### Inequality requirements 113| 114|**Inequality requirements** allow manually specifying a version range or an exact version to depend on. 115| 116|Here are some examples of inequality requirements: 117| 118|```text 119|>= 1.2.0 120|> 1 121|< 2 122|!= 1.2.3 123|``` 124| 125|#### Multiple requirements 126| 127|Multiple version requirements can also be separated with a comma, e.g. `>= 1.2, < 1.5`. 128| 129|### Exact requirements 130| 131|You can specify the exact version of a package. 132| 133|`1.2.3` is an example of an exact version specification. 134| 135|This will tell Poetry to install this version and this version only. 136|If other dependencies require a different version, the solver will ultimately fail and abort any installation or update procedures. 137| 138|Exact versions can also be specified with `==` according to [PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/). 139| 140|`==1.2.3` is an example of this. 141| 142|### Caret requirements 143| 144|{{% warning %}} 145|Not supported in `project.dependencies`. 146| 147|When using `poetry add` such constraints are automatically converted into an equivalent constraint. 148|{{% /warning %}} 149| 150|**Caret requirements** allow [SemVer](https://semver.org/) compatible updates to a specified version. An update is allowed if the new version number does not modify the left-most non-zero digit in the major, minor, patch grouping. For instance, if we previously ran `poetry add requests@^2.13.0` and wanted to update the library and ran `poetry update requests`, poetry would update us to version `2.14.0` if it was available, but would not update us to `3.0.0`. If instead, we had specified the version string as `^0.1.13`, poetry would update to `0.1.14` but not `0.2.0`. `0.0.x` is not considered compatible with any other version. 151| 152|Here are some more examples of caret requirements and the versions that would be allowed with them: 153| 154|| Requirement | Versions allowed | 155|| ----------- | ---------------- | 156|| ^1.2.3 | >=1.2.3 <2.0.0 | 157|| ^1.2 | >=1.2.0 <2.0.0 | 158|| ^1 | >=1.0.0 <2.0.0 | 159|| ^0.2.3 | >=0.2.3 <0.3.0 | 160|| ^0.0.3 | >=0.0.3 <0.0.4 | 161|| ^0.0 | >=0.0.0 <0.1.0 | 162|| ^0 | >=0.0.0 <1.0.0 | 163| 164|### Tilde requirements 165| 166|{{% warning %}} 167|Not supported in `project.dependencies`. 168| 169|When using `poetry add` such constraints are automatically converted into an equivalent constraint. 170|{{% /warning %}} 171| 172|**Tilde requirements** specify a minimal version with some ability to update. 173|If you specify a major, minor, and patch version or only a major and minor version, only patch-level changes are allowed. 174|If you only specify a major version, then minor- and patch-level changes are allowed. 175| 176|`~1.2.3` is an example of a tilde requirement. 177| 178|| Requirement | Versions allowed | 179|| ----------- | ---------------- | 180|| ~1.2.3 | >=1.2.3 <1.3.0 | 181|| ~1.2 | >=1.2.0 <1.3.0 | 182|| ~1 | >=1.0.0 <2.0.0 | 183| 184|### Using the `@` operator 185| 186|When adding dependencies via `poetry add`, you can use the `@` operator. 187|This is understood similarly to the `==` syntax, but also allows prefixing any 188|specifiers that are valid in `pyproject.toml`. For example: 189| 190|```shell 191|poetry add "django@^4.0.0" 192|``` 193| 194|The above would translate to the following entry in `pyproject.toml`: 195| 196|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="at-project" tabID2="at-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 197| 198|{{< tab tabID="at-project" >}} 199|```toml 200|[project] 201|# ... 202|dependencies = [ 203| "django (>=4.0.0,<5.0.0)", 204|] 205|``` 206| 207|{{< /tab >}} 208| 209|{{< tab tabID="at-poetry" >}} 210|```toml 211|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 212|django = "^4.0.0" 213|``` 214|{{< /tab >}} 215|{{< /tabs >}} 216| 217|The special keyword `latest` is also understood by the `@` operator: 218|```shell 219|poetry add django@latest 220|``` 221| 222|The above would translate to the following entry in `pyproject.toml`, assuming the latest release of `django` is `5.1.3`: 223| 224|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="at-latest-project" tabID2="at-latest-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 225| 226|{{< tab tabID="at-latest-project" >}} 227|```toml 228|[project] 229|# ... 230|dependencies = [ 231| "django (>=5.1.3,<6.0.0)", 232|] 233|``` 234|{{< /tab >}} 235| 236|{{< tab tabID="at-latest-poetry" >}} 237|```toml 238|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 239|django = "^5.1.3" 240|``` 241|{{< /tab >}} 242|{{< /tabs >}} 243| 244|#### Extras 245| 246|Extras and `@` can be combined as one might expect (`package[extra]@version`): 247| 248|```shell 249|poetry add django[bcrypt]@^4.0.0 250|``` 251| 252|## `git` dependencies 253| 254|To depend on a library located in a `git` repository, 255|the minimum information you need to specify is the location of the repository: 256| 257|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="git-project" tabID2="git-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 258| 259|{{< tab tabID="git-project" >}} 260|```toml 261|[project] 262|# ... 263|dependencies = [ 264| "requests @ git+https://github.com/requests/requests.git", 265|] 266|``` 267|{{< /tab >}} 268| 269|{{< tab tabID="git-poetry" >}} 270|In the `tool.poetry` section you use the `git` key: 271| 272|```toml 273|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 274|requests = { git = "https://github.com/requests/requests.git" } 275|``` 276| 277|{{< /tab >}} 278|{{< /tabs >}} 279| 280|Since we haven’t specified any other information, 281|Poetry assumes that we intend to use the latest commit on the `main` branch 282|to build our project. 283| 284|You can explicitly specify which branch, commit hash or tagged ref should be used: 285| 286|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="git-rev-project" tabID2="git-rev-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 287| 288|{{< tab tabID="git-rev-project" >}} 289|Append the information to the git url. 290| 291|```toml 292|[project] 293|# ... 294|dependencies = [ 295| "requests @ git+https://github.com/requests/requests.git@next", 296| "flask @ git+https://github.com/pallets/flask.git@38eb5d3b", 297| "numpy @ git+https://github.com/numpy/numpy.git@v0.13.2", 298|] 299|``` 300|{{< /tab >}} 301| 302|{{< tab tabID="git-rev-poetry" >}} 303|Combine the `git` key with the `branch`, `rev` or `tag` key respectively. 304| 305|```toml 306|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 307|# Get the latest revision on the branch named "next" 308|requests = { git = "https://github.com/kennethreitz/requests.git", branch = "next" } 309|# Get a revision by its commit hash 310|flask = { git = "https://github.com/pallets/flask.git", rev = "38eb5d3b" } 311|# Get a revision by its tag 312|numpy = { git = "https://github.com/numpy/numpy.git", tag = "v0.13.2" } 313|``` 314|{{< /tab >}} 315|{{< /tabs >}} 316| 317|It's possible to add a package that is located in a subdirectory of the VCS repository. 318| 319|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="git-subdir-project" tabID2="git-subdir-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 320| 321|{{< tab tabID="git-subdir-project" >}} 322|Provide the subdirectory as a URL fragment similarly to what [pip](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/vcs-support/#url-fragments) provides. 323|```toml 324|[project] 325|# ... 326|dependencies = [ 327| "subdir_package @ git+https://github.com/myorg/mypackage_with_subdirs.git#subdirectory=subdir" 328|] 329|``` 330|{{< /tab >}} 331| 332|{{< tab tabID="git-subdir-poetry" >}} 333|Use the `subdirectory` key in the `tool.poetry` section: 334| 335|```toml 336|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 337|# Install a package named `subdir_package` from a folder called `subdir` within the repository 338|subdir_package = { git = "https://github.com/myorg/mypackage_with_subdirs.git", subdirectory = "subdir" } 339|``` 340|{{< /tab >}} 341|{{< /tabs >}} 342| 343|The corresponding `add` call looks like this: 344| 345|```bash 346|poetry add "git+https://github.com/myorg/mypackage_with_subdirs.git#subdirectory=subdir" 347|``` 348| 349|To use an SSH connection, for example, in the case of private repositories, use the git+https://github.com/org/project.git 380|``` 381| 382|{{% note %}} 383|The default git client used is [Dulwich](https://www.dulwich.io/). 384| 385|We fall back to legacy system git client This fallback will be removed in 387|a future release where `gitcredentials` helpers can be better supported natively. 388| 389|In cases where you encounter issues with the default implementation, you may wish to 390|explicitly configure the use of the system git client via a shell subprocess call. 391| 392|```bash 393|poetry config system-git-client true 394|``` 395|{{% /note %}} 396| 397|## `path` dependencies 398| 399|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="path-project" tabID2="path-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 400| 401|{{< tab tabID="path-project" >}} 402|In the `project` section, you can only use absolute paths: 403| 404|```toml 405|[project] 406|# directory 407|dependencies = [ 408| "my-package @ file:///absolute/path/to/my-package" 409|] 410|# file 411|dependencies = [ 412| "my-package @ file:///absolute/path/to/my-package/dist/my-package-0.1.0.tar.gz" 413|] 414|``` 415|{{< /tab >}} 416| 417|{{< tab tabID="path-poetry" >}} 418|To depend on a library located in a local directory or file, 419|you can use the `path` property: 420| 421|```toml 422|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 423|# directory 424|my-package = { path = "../my-package/", develop = true } 425| 426|# file 427|my-package = { path = "../my-package/dist/my-package-0.1.0.tar.gz" } 428|``` 429| 430|To install directory path dependencies in editable mode, use the `develop` keyword and set it to `true`. 431|{{< /tab >}} 432|{{< /tabs >}} 433| 434|{{% note %}} 435|Path dependencies are intended for local development. 436|When building a wheel or sdist, Poetry records directory path dependencies as `file://` requirements, 437|which are not portable. %}} 503| 504|## `source` dependencies 505|{{% note %}} 506|It is not possible to define source dependencies in the `project` section. 507|{{% /note %}} 508| 509|To depend on a package from an [alternate repository]({{< relref "repositories#installing-from-private-package-sources" >}}), 510|you can use the `source` property: 511| 512|```toml 513|[[tool.poetry.source]] 514|name = "foo" 515|url = "https://foo.bar/simple/" 516|priority = "supplemental" 517| 518|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 519|my-cool-package = { version = "*", source = "foo" } 520|``` 521| 522|with the corresponding `add` call: 523| 524|```sh 525|poetry add my-cool-package --source foo 526|``` 527| 528|{{% note %}} 529|In this example, we expect `foo` to be configured correctly. See [using a private repository]({{< relref "repositories#installing-from-private-package-sources" >}}) 530|for further information. 531|{{% /note %}} 532| 533|## Python restricted dependencies 534| 535|You can also specify that a dependency should be installed only for specific Python versions: 536| 537|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="python-restriction-project" tabID2="python-restriction-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 538| 539|{{< tab tabID="python-restriction-project" >}} 540|```toml 541|[project] 542|# ... 543|dependencies = [ 544| "tomli (>=2.0.1,<3.0) ; python_version < '3.11'", 545| "pathlib2 (>=2.2,<3.0) ; python_version >= '3.9' and python_version < '4.0'" 546|] 547|``` 548|{{< /tab >}} 549| 550|{{< tab tabID="python-restriction-poetry" >}} 551| 552|```toml 553|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 554|tomli = { version = "^2.0.1", python = "<3.11" } 555|pathlib2 = { version = "^2.2", python = "^3.9" } 556|``` 557|{{< /tab >}} 558|{{< /tabs >}} 559| 560|## Using environment markers 561| 562|If you need more complex install conditions for your dependencies, 563|Poetry supports [environment markers](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0508/#environment-markers): 564| 565|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="markers-project" tabID2="markers-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 566| 567|{{< tab tabID="markers-project" >}} 568|```toml 569|[project] 570|# ... 571|dependencies = [ 572| "pathlib2 (>=2.2,<3.0) ; sys_platform == 'win32'" 595|] 596|``` 597| 598|`pathlib2` will be installed when you install your package with `--extras paths` on a `win32` machine. 599| 600|#### Exclusive extras 601| 602|{{% warning %}} 603|The first example will only work completely if you configure Poetry to not re-resolve for installation: 604| 605|```bash 606|poetry config installer.re-resolve false 607|``` 608| 609|This was a new feature of Poetry 2.0 and became the default behavior in Poetry 2.3. 610| 611|{{% /warning %}} 612| 613|Keep in mind that all combinations of possible extras available in your project need to be compatible with each other. 614|This means that in order to use differing or incompatible versions across different combinations, you need to make your 615|extra markers *exclusive*. For example, the following installs PyTorch from one source repository with CPU versions 616|when the `cuda` extra is *not* specified, while the other installs from another repository with a separate version set 617|for GPUs when the `cuda` extra *is* specified: 618| 619|```toml 620|[project] 621|name = "torch-example" 622|requires-python = ">=3.10" 623|dependencies = [ 624| "torch (==2.3.1+cpu) ; extra != 'cuda'", 625|] 626| 627|[project.optional-dependencies] 628|cuda = [ 629| "torch (==2.3.1+cu118)", 630|] 631| 632|[tool.poetry] 633|package-mode = false 634| 635|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 636|torch = [ 637| { markers = "extra != 'cuda'", source = "pytorch-cpu"}, 638| { markers = "extra == 'cuda'", source = "pytorch-cuda"}, 639| ] 640| 641|[[tool.poetry.source]] 642|name = "pytorch-cpu" 643|url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu" 644|priority = "explicit" 645| 646|[[tool.poetry.source]] 647|name = "pytorch-cuda" 648|url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118" 649|priority = "explicit" 650|``` 651| 652|For the CPU case, we have to specify `"extra != 'cuda'"` because the version specified is not compatible with the 653|GPU (`cuda`) version. 654| 655|This same logic applies when you want either-or extras: 656| 657|```toml 658|[project] 659|name = "torch-example" 660|requires-python = ">=3.10" 661| 662|[project.optional-dependencies] 663|cpu = [ 664| "torch (==2.3.1+cpu)", 665|] 666|cuda = [ 667| "torch (==2.3.1+cu118)", 668|] 669| 670|[tool.poetry] 671|package-mode = false 672| 673|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 674|torch = [ 675| { markers = "extra == 'cpu' and extra != 'cuda'", source = "pytorch-cpu"}, 676| { markers = "extra == 'cuda' and extra != 'cpu'", source = "pytorch-cuda"}, 677| ] 678| 679|[[tool.poetry.source]] 680|name = "pytorch-cpu" 681|url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu" 682|priority = "explicit" 683| 684|[[tool.poetry.source]] 685|name = "pytorch-cuda" 686|url = "https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118" 687|priority = "explicit" 688|``` 689| 690|## Multiple constraints dependencies 691| 692|Sometimes, one of your dependencies may have different version ranges depending 693|on the target Python versions. 694| 695|Let's say you have a dependency on the package `foo` which is only compatible 696|with Python 3.6–3.7 up to version 1.9, and compatible with Python 3.8+ from version 2.0: 697|you would declare it like so: 698| 699|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="multiple-constraints-project" tabID2="multiple-constraints-poetry" tabName1="[project]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 700| 701|{{< tab tabID="multiple-constraints-project" >}} 702|```toml 703|[project] 704|# ... 705|dependencies = [ 706| "foo (<=1.9) ; python_version >= '3.6' and python_version < '3.8'", 707| "foo (>=2.0,<3.0) ; python_version >= '3.8'" 708|] 709|``` 710|{{< /tab >}} 711| 712|{{< tab tabID="multiple-constraints-poetry" >}} 713|```toml 714|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 715|foo = [ 716| {version = "<=1.9", python = ">=3.6,<3.8"}, 717| {version = "^2.0", python = ">=3.8"} 718|] 719|``` 720|{{< /tab >}} 721|{{< /tabs >}} 722| 723|{{% note %}} 724|The constraints **must** have different requirements (like `python`) 725|otherwise it will cause an error when resolving dependencies. 726|{{% /note %}} 727| 728|### Combining git / url / path dependencies with source repositories 729| 730|Direct origin (`git`/ `url`/ `path`) dependencies can satisfy the requirement of a dependency that 731|doesn't explicitly specify a source, even when mutually exclusive markers are used. For instance, 732|in the following example, the url package will also be a valid solution for the second requirement: 733|```toml 734|foo = [ 735| { platform = "darwin", url = "https://example.com/example-1.0-py3-none-any.whl" }, 736| { platform = "linux", version = "^1.0" }, 737|] 738|``` 739| 740|Sometimes you may instead want to use a direct origin dependency for specific conditions 741|(i.e., a compiled package that is not available on PyPI for a certain platform/architecture) while 742|falling back on source repositories in other cases. In this case you should explicitly ask for your 743|dependency to be satisfied by another `source`. For example: 744|```toml 745|foo = [ 746| { platform = "darwin", url = "https://example.com/foo-1.0.0-py3-none-macosx_11_0_arm64.whl" }, 747| { platform = "linux", version = "^1.0", source = "pypi" }, 748|] 749|``` 750| 751|## Expanded dependency specification syntax 752| 753|In the case of more complex dependency specifications, you may find that you 754|end up with lines which are very long and difficult to read. In these cases, 755|you can shift from using "inline table" syntax to the "standard table" syntax. 756| 757|An example where this might be useful is the following: 758| 759|```toml 760|[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies] 761|black = {version = "19.10b0", allow-prereleases = true, python = "^3.7", markers = "platform_python_implementation == 'CPython'"} 762|``` 763| 764|As a single line, this is a lot to digest. To make this a bit easier to 765|work with, you can do the following: 766| 767|```toml 768|[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies.black] 769|version = "19.10b0" 770|allow-prereleases = true 771|python = "^3.7" 772|markers = "platform_python_implementation == 'CPython'" 773|``` 774| 775|The same information is still present, and ends up providing the exact 776|same specification. It's simply split into multiple, slightly more readable, 777|lines. 778| 779|### Handling of pre-releases 780| 781|Per default, Poetry will prefer stable releases and only choose a pre-release 782|if no stable release satisfies a version constraint. In some cases, this may result in 783|a solution containing pre-releases even if another solution without pre-releases exists. 784| 785|If you want to disallow pre-releases for a specific dependency, 786|you can set `allow-prereleases` to `false`. In this case, dependency resolution will 787|fail if there is no solution without choosing a pre-release. 788| 789|If you want to prefer the latest version of a dependency even if it is a pre-release, 790|you can set `allow-prereleases` to `true` so that Poetry makes no distinction 791|between stable and pre-release versions during dependency resolution. --- END FILE: 10|--- 11| 12|# Configuration 13| 14|Poetry can be configured via the `config` command ([see more about its usage here]({{< relref "cli#config" >}} "config command documentation")) 15|or directly in the `config.toml` file that will be automatically created when you first run that command. 16|This file can typically be found in one of the following directories: 17| 18|- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pypoetry` 19|- Windows: `%APPDATA%\pypoetry` 20| 21|For Unix, we follow the XDG spec and support `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`. 22|That means, by default `~/.config/pypoetry`. 23| 24|## Local configuration 25| 26|Poetry also provides the ability to have settings that are specific to a project 27|by passing the `--local` option to the `config` command. 28| 29|```bash 30|poetry config virtualenvs.create false --local 31|``` 32| 33|{{% note %}} 34|Your local configuration of Poetry application is stored in the `poetry.toml` file, 35|which is separate from `pyproject.toml`. 36|{{% /note %}} 37| 38|{{% note %}} 39|If a setting is defined in both `poetry.toml` (local/project) and `config.toml` (global), 40|the local/project configuration takes precedence over the global configuration. 41|{{% /note %}} 42| 43|{{% warning %}} 44|Be mindful when checking in this file into your repository since it may contain user-specific or sensitive information. 45|{{% /warning %}} 46| 47|## Listing the current configuration 48| 49|To list the current configuration you can use the `--list` option 50|of the `config` command: 51| 52|```bash 53|poetry config --list 54|``` 55| 56|which will give you something similar to this: 57| 58|```toml 59|cache-dir = "/path/to/cache/directory" 60|virtualenvs.create = true 61|virtualenvs.in-project = null 62|virtualenvs.options.always-copy = true 63|virtualenvs.options.no-pip = false 64|virtualenvs.options.system-site-packages = false 65|virtualenvs.path = "{cache-dir}/virtualenvs" # /path/to/cache/directory/virtualenvs 66|virtualenvs.prompt = "{project_name}-py{python_version}" 67|virtualenvs.use-poetry-python = false 68|``` 69| 70|## Displaying a single configuration setting 71| 72|If you want to see the value of a specific setting, you can 73|give its name to the `config` command 74| 75|```bash 76|poetry config virtualenvs.path 77|``` 78| 79|For a full list of the supported settings see [Available settings](#available-settings). 80| 81|## Adding or updating a configuration setting 82| 83|To change or otherwise add a new configuration setting, you can pass 84|a value after the setting's name: 85| 86|```bash 87|poetry config virtualenvs.path /path/to/cache/directory/virtualenvs 88|``` 89| 90|For a full list of the supported settings see [Available settings](#available-settings). 91| 92|## Removing a specific setting 93| 94|If you want to remove a previously set setting, you can use the `--unset` option: 95| 96|```bash 97|poetry config virtualenvs.path --unset 98|``` 99| 100|The setting will then retrieve its default value. 101| 102|## Using environment variables 103| 104|Sometimes, in particular when using Poetry with CI tools, it's easier 105|to use environment variables and not have to execute configuration commands. 106| 107|Poetry supports this and any setting can be set by using environment variables. 108| 109|The environment variables must be prefixed by `POETRY_` and are comprised of the uppercase 110|name of the setting and with dots and dashes replaced by underscore, here is an example: 111| 112|```bash 113|export POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_PATH=/path/to/virtualenvs/directory 114|``` 115| 116|This also works for secret settings, like credentials: 117| 118|```bash 119|export POETRY_HTTP_BASIC_MY_REPOSITORY_PASSWORD=secret 120|``` 121| 122|## Configuration sources 123| 124|When a setting is set in multiple places, Poetry applies the following precedence 125|(from highest to lowest): 126| 127|1. Environment variables (for example, `POETRY_VIRTUALENVS_CREATE`) 128|2. The local `poetry.toml` file (created with `poetry config --local`) 129|3. The global `config.toml` file 130|4. The setting's default value 131| 132|For repository credentials (`http-basic.*`, `pypi-token.*`), Poetry may also read 133|from `auth.toml` and the system keyring (for details see [Repositories]({{< relref "repositories" >}})). 134|Environment variables still take precedence over file-based values. 135| 136|## Migrate outdated configs 137| 138|If Poetry renames or remove config options it might be necessary to migrate explicit set options. This is possible 139|by running: 140| 141|```bash 142|poetry config --migrate 143|``` 144| 145|If you need to migrate a local config run: 146| 147|```bash 148|poetry config --migrate --local 149|``` 150| 151|## Default Directories 152| 153|Poetry uses the following default directories: 154| 155|### Config Directory 156| 157|- Linux: `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/pypoetry` or `~/.config/pypoetry` 158|- Windows: `%APPDATA%\pypoetry` 159|- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pypoetry` 160| 161|You can override the config directory by setting the `POETRY_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable. 162| 163|### Data Directory 164| 165|- Linux: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/pypoetry` or `~/.local/share/pypoetry` 166|- Windows: `%APPDATA%\pypoetry` 167|- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pypoetry` 168| 169|You can override the data directory by setting the `POETRY_DATA_DIR` or `POETRY_HOME` environment variables. If `POETRY_HOME` is set, it will be given higher priority. 170| 171|### Cache Directory 172| 173|- Linux: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/pypoetry` or `~/.cache/pypoetry` 174|- Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\pypoetry` 175|- macOS: `~/Library/Caches/pypoetry` 176| 177|You can override the cache directory by setting the `POETRY_CACHE_DIR` environment variable. 178| 179|## Available settings 180| 181|### `cache-dir` 182| 183|**Type**: `string` 184| 185|**Environment Variable**: `POETRY_CACHE_DIR` 186| 187|The path to the cache directory used by Poetry. 188| 189|Defaults to one of the following directories: 190| 191|- macOS: `~/Library/Caches/pypoetry` 192|- Windows: `C:\Users\\AppData\Local\pypoetry\Cache` 193|- Unix: `~/.cache/pypoetry` 194| 195|### `data-dir` 196| 197|**Type**: `string` 198| 199|**Environment Variable**: `POETRY_DATA_DIR` 200| 201|The path to the data directory used by Poetry. 202| 203|- Linux: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/pypoetry` or `~/.local/share/pypoetry` 204|- Windows: `%APPDATA%\pypoetry` 205|- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/pypoetry` 206| 207|You can override the data directory by setting the `POETRY_DATA_DIR` or `POETRY_HOME` environment variables. But, you want to 29|install a dependency to your project for a [simple API repository](#simple-api-repository)? Let's 30|do it. 31| 32|First, [configure](#project-configuration) the [package source](#package-sources) as a [supplemental](#supplemental-package-sources) (or [explicit](#explicit-package-sources)) package source to your 33|project. 34| 35|```bash 36|poetry source add --priority=supplemental foo https://pypi.example.org/simple/ 37|``` 38| 39|Then, assuming the repository requires authentication, configure credentials for it. 40| 41|```bash 42|poetry config http-basic.foo 43|``` 44|{{% warning %}} 45|If you have completed configuring credentials and are receiving authorization failures, check for the presence of `~/.netrc`, which has been known to conflict with Poetry's configured authentication. 46|{{% /warning %}} 47| 48|{{% warning %}} 49|Depending on your system configuration, credentials might be saved in your command line history. 50|Many shells do not save commands to history when they are prefixed by a space character. For more information, please refer to your shell's documentation. 51|{{% /warning %}} 52| 53|{{% note %}} 54|If you would like to provide the password interactively, you can simply omit `` in your command. And 55|Poetry will prompt you to enter the credential manually. 56| 57|```bash 58|poetry config http-basic.foo 59|``` 60|{{% /note %}} 61| 62|Once this is done, you can add dependencies to your project from this source. 63| 64|```bash 65|poetry add --source foo private-package 66|``` 67| 68|#### Publishing to a private repository 69| 70|Great, now all that is left is to publish your package. Assuming you'd want to share it privately 71|with your team, you can configure the 72|[Upload API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/upload/) endpoint for your 73|[publishable repository](#publishable-repositories). 74| 75|```bash 76|poetry config repositories.foo https://pypi.example.org/legacy/ 77|``` 78| 79|{{% note %}} 80| 81|If you need to use a different credential for your [package source](#package-sources), then it is 82|recommended to use a different name for your publishing repository. 83| 84|```bash 85|poetry config repositories.foo-pub https://pypi.example.org/legacy/ 86|poetry config http-basic.foo-pub 87|``` 88| 89|{{% /note %}} 90| 91|{{% note %}} 92|When configuring a repository using environment variables, note that correct suffixes need to be used. 93| 94|```bash 95|export POETRY_REPOSITORIES_FOO_URL=https://pypi.example.org/legacy/ 96|export POETRY_HTTP_BASIC_FOO_USERNAME= 97|export POETRY_HTTP_BASIC_FOO_PASSWORD= 98|``` 99|{{% /note %}} 100| 101|Now, all that is left is to build and publish your project using the 102|[`publish`]({{< relref "cli#publish" >}}). 103| 104|```bash 105|poetry publish --build --repository foo-pub 106|``` 107| 108|## Package Sources 109| 110|By default, if you have not configured any primary source, 111|Poetry is configured to use the Python ecosystem's canonical package index 112|[PyPI](https://pypi.org). 113|You can alter this behavior and exclusively look up packages only from the configured 114|package sources by adding at least one primary source. 115| 116|{{% note %}} 117| 118|Except for the implicitly configured source for [PyPI](https://pypi.org) named `PyPI`, 119|package sources are local to a project and must be configured within the project's 120|[`pyproject.toml`]({{< relref "pyproject" >}}) file. This is **not** the same configuration used 121|when publishing a package. 122| 123|{{% /note %}} 124| 125|{{% warning %}} 126| 127|Package sources are a Poetry-specific feature and **not** included in 128|[core metadata](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/core-metadata/) produced by 129|the poetry-core build backend. 130| 131|Consequently, when a Poetry project is e.g., installed using Pip (as a normal package or in editable 132|mode), package sources will be ignored and the dependencies in question downloaded from PyPI by 133|default. 134| 135|{{% /warning %}} 136| 137|### Project Configuration 138| 139|These package sources may be managed using the [`source`]({{< relref "cli#source" >}}) command for 140|your project. 141| 142|```bash 143|poetry source add foo https://foo.bar/simple/ 144|``` 145| 146|{{% note %}} 147| 148|If your package source requires [credentials](#configuring-credentials) or 149|[certificates](#certificates), please refer to the relevant sections below. 150| 151|{{% /note %}} 152| 153|This will generate the following configuration snippet in your 154|[`pyproject.toml`]({{< relref "pyproject" >}}) file. 155| 156|```toml 157|[[tool.poetry.source]] 158|name = "foo" 159|url = "https://foo.bar/simple/" 160|priority = "primary" 161|``` 162| 163|If `priority` is undefined, the source is considered a primary source, 164|which disables the implicit PyPI source and takes precedence over supplemental sources. 165| 166|Package sources are considered in the following order: 167|1. [primary sources](#primary-package-sources) or implicit PyPI (if there are no primary sources), 168|2. [supplemental sources](#supplemental-package-sources). 169| 170|[Explicit sources](#explicit-package-sources) are considered only for packages that explicitly [indicate their source](#package-source-constraint). 171| 172|Within each priority class, package sources are considered in order of appearance in `pyproject.toml`. 173| 174| 175|#### Primary Package Sources 176| 177|All primary package sources are searched for each dependency without a [source constraint](#package-source-constraint). 178|If you configure at least one primary source, the implicit PyPI source is disabled. 179| 180|```bash 181|poetry source add --priority=primary foo https://foo.bar/simple/ 182|``` 183| 184|Sources without a priority are considered primary sources, too. 185| 186|```bash 187|poetry source add foo https://foo.bar/simple/ 188|``` 189| 190|{{% warning %}} 191| 192|The implicit PyPI source is disabled automatically if at least one primary source is configured. 193|If you want to use PyPI in addition to a primary source, configure it explicitly 194|with a certain priority, e.g. 195| 196|```bash 197|poetry source add --priority=primary PyPI 198|``` 199| 200|This way, the priority of PyPI can be set in a fine-granular way. 201| 202|The equivalent specification in `pyproject.toml` is: 203| 204|```toml 205|[[tool.poetry.source]] 206|name = "pypi" 207|priority = "primary" 208|``` 209| 210|**Omit the `url` when specifying PyPI explicitly.** Because PyPI is internally configured 211|with Poetry, the PyPI repository cannot be configured with a given URL. Remember, you can always use 212|`poetry check` to ensure the validity of the `pyproject.toml` file. 213| 214|{{% /warning %}} 215| 216| 217|#### Supplemental Package Sources 218| 219|*Introduced in 1.5.0* 220| 221|Package sources configured as supplemental are only searched if no other (higher-priority) source yields a compatible package distribution. This is particularly convenient if the response time of the source is high and relatively few package distributions are to be fetched from this source. 222| 223|You can configure a package source as a supplemental source with `priority = "supplemental"` in your package 224|source configuration. 225| 226|```bash 227|poetry source add --priority=supplemental foo https://foo.bar/simple/ 228|``` 229| 230|There can be more than one supplemental package source. 231| 232|{{% warning %}} 233| 234|Take into account that someone could publish a new package to a primary source 235|which matches a package in your supplemental source. They could coincidentally 236|or intentionally replace your dependency with something you did not expect. 237| 238|{{% /warning %}} 239| 240| 241|#### Explicit Package Sources 242| 243|*Introduced in 1.5.0* 244| 245|If package sources are configured as explicit, these sources are only searched when a package configuration [explicitly indicates](#package-source-constraint) that it should be found on this package source. 246| 247|You can configure a package source as an explicit source with `priority = "explicit"` in your package source configuration. 248| 249|```bash 250|poetry source add --priority=explicit foo https://foo.bar/simple/ 251|``` 252| 253|There can be more than one explicit package source. 254| 255|{{% note %}} 256|A real-world example where an explicit package source is useful, is for PyTorch GPU packages. 257| 258|```bash 259|poetry source add --priority=explicit pytorch-gpu-src https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118 260|poetry add --source pytorch-gpu-src torch torchvision torchaudio 261|``` 262|{{% /note %}} 263| 264|#### Package Source Constraint 265| 266|All package sources (including possibly supplemental sources) will be searched 267|during the package lookup process. 268|These network requests will occur for all primary sources, regardless of if the package is 269|found at one or more sources, and all supplemental sources until the package is found. 270| 271|In order to limit the search for a specific package to a particular package repository, you can specify the source explicitly. 272| 273|```bash 274|poetry add --source internal-pypi httpx 275|``` 276| 277|This results in the following configuration in `pyproject.toml`: 278| 279|```toml 280|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 281|... 282|httpx = { version = "^0.22", source = "internal-pypi" } 283| 284|[[tool.poetry.source]] 285|name = "internal-pypi" 286|url = ... 287|priority = ... 288|``` 289| 290|{{% note %}} 291| 292|A repository that is configured to be the only source for retrieving a certain package can itself have any priority. 293|In particular, it does not need to have priority `"explicit"`. 294|If a repository is configured to be the source of a package, it will be the only source that is considered for that package 295|and the repository priority will have no effect on the resolution. 296| 297|{{% /note %}} 298| 299|{{% note %}} 300| 301|Package `source` keys are not inherited by their dependencies. 302|In particular, if `package-A` is configured to be found in `source = internal-pypi`, 303|and `package-A` depends on `package-B` that is also to be found on `internal-pypi`, 304|then `package-B` needs to be configured as such in `pyproject.toml`. 305|The easiest way to achieve this is to add `package-B` with a wildcard constraint: 306| 307|```bash 308|poetry add --source internal-pypi package-B@* 309|``` 310| 311|This will ensure that `package-B` is searched only in the `internal-pypi` package source. 312|The version constraints on `package-B` are derived from `package-A` (and other client packages), as usual. 313| 314|If you want to avoid additional main dependencies, 315|you can add `package-B` to a dedicated [dependency group]({{< relref "managing-dependencies#dependency-groups" >}}): 316| 317|```bash 318|poetry add --group explicit --source internal-pypi package-B@* 319|``` 320| 321|{{% /note %}} 322| 323|{{% note %}} 324| 325|Package source constraints are strongly suggested for all packages that are expected 326|to be provided only by one specific source to avoid dependency confusion attacks. 327| 328|{{% /note %}} 329| 330|### Supported Package Sources 331| 332|#### Python Package Index (PyPI) 333| 334|Poetry interacts with [PyPI](https://pypi.org) via its 335|[JSON API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/json/). This is used to retrieve a requested 336|package's versions, metadata, files, etc. 337| 338|{{% note %}} 339| 340|If the package's published metadata is invalid, Poetry will download the available bdist/sdist to 341|inspect it locally to identify the relevant metadata. 342| 343|{{% /note %}} 344| 345|If you want to explicitly select a package from [PyPI](https://pypi.org) you can use the `--source` 346|option with the [`add`]({{< relref "cli#add" >}}) command, like shown below. 347| 348|```bash 349|poetry add --source pypi httpx@^0.22.0 350|``` 351| 352|This will generate the following configuration snippet in your `pyproject.toml` file. 353| 354|```toml 355|httpx = {version = "^0.22.0", source = "pypi"} 356|``` 357| 358|{{% warning %}} 359| 360|The implicit `PyPI` source will be disabled and not used for any packages 361|if at least one [primary source](#primary-package-sources) is configured. 362| 363|{{% /warning %}} 364| 365|#### Simple API Repository 366| 367|Poetry can fetch and install package dependencies from public or private custom repositories that 368|implement the simple repository API as described in [PEP 503](https://peps.python.org/pep-0503/). 369| 370|{{% warning %}} 371| 372|When using sources that distribute large wheels without providing file checksum in file URLs, 373|Poetry will download each candidate wheel at least once in order to generate the checksum. This can 374|manifest as long dependency resolution times when adding packages from this source. 375| 376|{{% /warning %}} 377| 378|These package sources may be configured via the following command in your project. 379| 380|```bash 381|poetry source add testpypi https://test.pypi.org/simple/ 382|``` 383| 384|{{% note %}} 385| 386|Note the trailing `/simple/`. This is important when configuring 387|[PEP 503](https://peps.python.org/pep-0503/) compliant package sources. 388| 389|{{% /note %}} 390| 391|In addition to [PEP 503](https://peps.python.org/pep-0503/), Poetry can also handle simple API 392|repositories that implement [PEP 658](https://peps.python.org/pep-0658/) (*Introduced in 1.2.0*). 393|This is helpful in reducing dependency resolution time for packages from these sources as Poetry can 394|avoid having to download each candidate distribution, in order to determine associated metadata. 395| 396|{{% note %}} 397| 398|*Why does Poetry insist on downloading all candidate distributions for all platforms when metadata 399|is not available?* 400| 401|The need for this stems from the fact that Poetry's lock file is platform-agnostic. This means, in 402|order to resolve dependencies for a project, Poetry needs metadata for all platform-specific 403|distributions. And when this metadata is not readily available, downloading the distribution and 404|inspecting it locally is the only remaining option. 405| 406|{{% /note %}} 407| 408|#### Single Page Link Source 409| 410|*Introduced in 1.2.0* 411| 412|Some projects choose to release their binary distributions via a single page link source that 413|partially follows the structure of a package page in [PEP 503](https://peps.python.org/pep-0503/). 414| 415|These package sources may be configured via the following command in your project. 416| 417|```bash 418|poetry source add jax https://storage.googleapis.com/jax-releases/jax_releases.html 419|``` 420| 421|{{% note %}} 422| 423|All caveats regarding slower resolution times described for simple API repositories do apply here as 424|well. 425| 426|{{% /note %}} 427| 428| 429|## Publishable Repositories 430| 431|Poetry treats repositories to which you publish packages as user-specific and not project-specific 432|configuration unlike [package sources](#package-sources). Poetry, today, only supports the 433|[Legacy Upload API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/upload/) when publishing 434|your project. 435| 436|These are configured using the [`config`]({{< relref "cli#config" >}}) command, under the 437|`repositories` key. 438| 439|```bash 440|poetry config repositories.testpypi https://test.pypi.org/legacy/ 441|``` 442| 443|{{% note %}} 444| 445|[Legacy Upload API](https://docs.pypi.org/api/upload/) URLs are 446|typically different to the same one provided by the repository for the simple API. You'll note that 447|in the example of [Test PyPI](https://test.pypi.org/), both the host (`test.pypi.org`) as 448|well as the path (`/legacy`) are different to its simple API (`https://test.pypi.org/simple`). 449| 450|While the examples show URLs with a trailing slash (e.g., `https://test.pypi.org/legacy/`), Poetry automatically normalizes legacy repository URLs by adding a trailing slash if one is missing. In the above example, the credential will be stored using the name `poetry-repository-pypi`. If access to keyring fails or is unsupported, this will fall back to writing the password to the `auth.toml` file along with the username. 493| 494|Keyring support is enabled using the [keyring library](https://pypi.org/project/keyring/). The following will configure the "foo" repository to validate the repository's 551|certificate using a custom certificate authority and use a client certificate (note that these config variables do not 552|both need to be set): 553| 554|```bash 555|poetry config certificates.foo.cert /path/to/ca.pem 556|poetry config certificates.foo.client-cert /path/to/client.pem 557|``` 558| 559|{{% note %}} 560|The value of `certificates..cert` can be set to `false` if certificate verification is 561|required to be skipped. certificate verification is not recommended as it does not conform to security 570|best practices. 571|{{% /warning %}} 572|{{% /note %}} 573| 574|## Caches 575| 576|Poetry employs multiple caches for package sources in order to improve user experience and avoid duplicate network 577|requests. 578| 579|The first level cache is a [Cache-Control](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Cache-Control) 580|header-based cache for almost all HTTP requests. 581| 582|Further, every HTTP backed package source caches metadata associated with a package once it is fetched or generated. 583|Additionally, downloaded files (package distributions) are also cached. 584| 585|## Debugging Issues 586|If you encounter issues with package sources, one of the simplest steps you might take to debug an issue is rerunning 587|your command with the `--no-cache` flag. 588| 589|```bash 590|poetry --no-cache add pycowsay 591|``` 592| 593|If this solves your issue, you can consider clearing your cache using the [`cache`]({{< relref "cli#cache-clear" >}}) 594|command. 595| 596|Alternatively, you could also consider enabling
