3|draft: false 4|type: docs 5|layout: single 6| 7|menu: 8| docs: 9| weight: 110 10|--- 11| 12|# FAQ 13| 14|### Why is the dependency resolution process slow? 15| 16|While the dependency resolver at the heart of Poetry is highly optimized and 17|should be fast enough for most cases, with certain sets of dependencies, 18|it can take time to find a valid solution. 19| 20|This is due to the fact that not all libraries on PyPI have properly declared their metadata 21|and, as such, they are not available via the PyPI JSON API. At this point, Poetry has no choice 22|but to download the packages and inspect them to get the necessary information. This is an expensive 23|operation, both in bandwidth and time, which is why it seems this is a long process. 24| 25|At the moment, there is no way around it. However, if you notice that Poetry 26|is downloading many versions of a single package, you can lessen the workload 27|by constraining that one package in your pyproject.toml more narrowly. That way, 28|Poetry does not have to sift through so many versions of it, which may speed up 29|the locking process considerably in some cases. 30| 31|{{% note %}} 32|Once Poetry has cached the releases' information on your machine, the dependency resolution process 33|will be much faster. 34|{{% /note %}} 35| 36|### What kind of versioning scheme does Poetry use for itself? 37| 38|Poetry uses "major.minor.micro" version identifiers as mentioned in 39|[PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440/#final-releases). 40| 41|Version bumps are done similar to Python's versioning: 42|* A major version bump (incrementing the first number) is only done for breaking changes 43| if a deprecation cycle is not possible, and many users have to perform some manual steps 44| to migrate from one version to the next one. 45|* A minor version bump (incrementing the second number) may include new features as well 46| as new deprecations and drop features deprecated in an earlier minor release. 47|* A micro version bump (incrementing the third number) usually only includes bug fixes. 48| Deprecated features will not be dropped in a micro release. 49| 50|### Why does Poetry not adhere to semantic versioning? 51| 52|Because of its large user base, even small changes not considered relevant by most users 53|can turn out to be a breaking change for some users in hindsight. 54|Sticking to strict [semantic versioning](https://semver.org) and (almost) always bumping 55|the major version instead of the minor version does not seem desirable 56|since the minor version will not carry any meaning anymore. 57| 58|### Are unbound version constraints a bad idea? 59| 60|A version constraint without an upper bound such as `*` or `>=3.4` will allow updates to any future version of the dependency. 61|This includes major versions breaking backward compatibility. 62| 63|Once a release of your package is published, you cannot tweak its dependencies anymore in case a dependency breaks BC 64|– you have to do a new release but the previous one stays broken. 65|(Users can still work around the broken dependency by restricting it by themselves.) 66| 67|To avoid such issues, you can define an upper bound on your constraints, 68|which you can increase in a new release after testing that your package is compatible 69|with the new major version of your dependency. 70| 71|For example, instead of using `>=3.4` you can use `^3.4` which allows all versions `<4.0`. 72|The `^` operator works very well with libraries following [semantic versioning](https://semver.org). 73| 74|However, when defining an upper bound, users of your package are not able to update 75|a dependency beyond the upper bound even if it does not break anything 76|and is fully compatible with your package. 77|You have to release a new version of your package with an increased upper-bound first. 78| 79|If your package is used as a library in other packages, it might be better to avoid 80|upper bounds and thus unnecessary dependency conflicts (unless you already know for sure 81|that the next release of the dependency will break your package). 82|If your package is used as an application, it might be worth defining an upper bound. 83| 84|### Is tox supported? 85| 86|**Yes**. Provided that you are using `tox` >= 4, you can use it in combination with 87|the PEP 517 compliant build system provided by Poetry. (With tox 3, you have to set the 88|[isolated build](https://tox.wiki/en/3.27.1/config.html#conf-isolated_build) option.) 89| 90|So, in your `pyproject.toml` file, add this section if it does not already exist: 91| 92|```toml 93|[build-system] 94|requires = ["poetry-core>=1.0.0"] 95|build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api" 96|``` 97| 98|`tox` can be configured in multiple ways. It depends on what should be the code under test and which dependencies 99|should be installed. 100| 101|#### Use case #1 102|```ini 103|[tox] 104| 105|[testenv] 106|deps = 107| pytest 108|commands = 109| pytest tests/ --import-mode importlib 110|``` 111| 112|`tox` will create an `sdist` package of the project and uses `pip` to install it in a fresh environment. 113|Thus, dependencies are resolved by `pip`. 114| 115|#### Use case #2 116|```ini 117|[tox] 118| 119|[testenv] 120|allowlist_externals = poetry 121|commands_pre = 122| poetry install --no-root --sync 123|commands = 124| poetry run pytest tests/ --import-mode importlib 125|``` 126| 127|`tox` will create an `sdist` package of the project and uses `pip` to install it in a fresh environment. 128|Thus, dependencies are resolved by `pip` in the first place. But afterward, we run Poetry, 129| which will install the locked dependencies into the environment. 130| 131|#### Use case #3 132|```ini 133|[tox] 134| 135|[testenv] 136|skip_install = true 137|allowlist_externals = poetry 138|commands_pre = 139| poetry install 140|commands = 141| poetry run pytest tests/ --import-mode importlib 142|``` 143| 144|`tox` will not do any install. Poetry installs all the dependencies and the current package in editable mode. 145|Thus, tests are running against the local files and not the built and installed package. 146| 147|#### Note about credentials 148| 149|Note that `tox` does not forward the environment variables of your current shell session by default. 150|This may cause Poetry to not be able to install dependencies in the `tox` environments if you have configured 151|credentials using the system keyring on Linux systems or using environment variables in general. 152|You can use the `passenv` [configuration option](https://tox.wiki/en/latest/config.html#passenv) to forward the 153|required variables explicitly or `passenv = "*"` to forward all of them. 154|Linux systems may require forwarding the `DBUS_SESSION_BUS_ADDRESS` variable to allow access to the system keyring, 155|though this may vary between desktop environments. 156| 157|Alternatively, you can disable the keyring completely: 158| 159|```bash 160|poetry config keyring.enabled false 161|``` 162| 163|Be aware that this will cause Poetry to write passwords to plaintext config files. 164|You will need to set the credentials again after changing this setting. 165| 166|### Is Nox supported? 167| 168|Use the [`nox-poetry`](https://github.com/cjolowicz/nox-poetry) package to install locked versions of 169|dependencies specified in `poetry.lock` into [Nox](https://nox.thea.codes/en/stable/) sessions. 170| 171|### I don't want Poetry to manage my virtual environments. Can I disable it? 172| 173|While Poetry automatically creates virtual environments to always work isolated 174|from the global Python installation, there are rare scenarios where the use of a Poetry managed 175|virtual environment is not possible or preferred. 176| 177|In this case, you can disable this feature by setting the `virtualenvs.create` setting to `false`: 178| 179|```bash 180|poetry config virtualenvs.create false 181|``` 182| 183|{{% warning %}} 184|The recommended best practice, including when installing an application within a container, is to make 185|use of a virtual environment. This can also be managed by another tool. 186| 187|The Poetry team strongly encourages the use of a virtual environment. 188|{{% /warning %}} 189| 190|### Why is Poetry telling me that the current project's supported Python range is not compatible with one or more packages' Python requirements? 191| 192|Unlike `pip`, Poetry doesn't resolve for just the Python in the current environment. Instead, it makes sure that a dependency 193|is resolvable within the given Python version range in `pyproject.toml`. 194| 195|Assume you have the following `pyproject.toml`: 196| 197|```toml 198|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 199|python = "^3.7" 200|``` 201| 202|This means your project aims to be compatible with any Python version >=3.7,<4.0. Whenever you try to add a dependency 203|whose Python requirement doesn't match the whole range, Poetry will tell you this, e.g.: 204| 205|``` 206|The current project's supported Python range (>=3.7.0,<4.0.0) is not compatible with some of the required packages Python requirement: 207| - scipy requires Python >=3.7,<3.11, so it will not be installable for Python >=3.11,<4.0.0 208|``` 209| 210|Usually you will want to match the supported Python range of your project with the upper bound of the failing dependency. 211|Alternatively, you can tell Poetry to install this dependency [only for a specific range of Python versions]({{< relref "dependency-specification#multiple-constraints-dependencies" >}}), 212|if you know that it's not needed in all versions. 213| 214|If you do not want to set an upper bound in the metadata when building your project, 215|you can omit it in the `project` section and only set it in `tool.poetry.dependencies`: 216| 217|```toml 218|[project] 219|# ... 220|requires-python = ">=3.7" # used for metadata when building the project 221| 222|[tool.poetry.dependencies] 223|python = ">=3.7,<3.11" # used for locking dependencies 224|``` 225| 226| 227|### Why does Poetry enforce PEP 440 versions? 228| 229|This is done to be compliant with the broader Python ecosystem. 230| 231|For example, if Poetry builds a distribution for a project that uses a version that is not valid, according to 232|[PEP 440](https://peps.python.org/pep-0440), third party tools will be unable to parse the version correctly. 233| 234| 235|### Poetry busts my Docker cache because it requires me to COPY my source files in before installing 3rd party dependencies 236| 237|By default, running `poetry install ...` requires you to have your source files present (both the "root" package and any directory path dependencies you might have). 238|This interacts poorly with Docker's caching mechanisms because any change to a source file will make any layers (subsequent commands in your Dockerfile) re-run. 239|For example, you might have a Dockerfile that looks something like this: 240| 241|```text 242|FROM python 243|COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock . 244|COPY src/ ./src 245|RUN pip install poetry && poetry install --only main 246|``` 247| 248|As soon as *any* source file changes, the cache for the `RUN` layer will be invalidated, which forces all 3rd party dependencies (likely the slowest step out of these) to be installed again if you changed any files in `src/`. 249| 250|To avoid this cache busting you can split this into two steps: 251| 252|1. Install 3rd party dependencies. 253|2. Copy over your source code and install just the source code. 254| 255|This might look something like this: 256| 257|```text 258|FROM python 259|COPY pyproject.toml poetry.lock . 260|RUN pip install poetry && poetry install --only main --no-root --no-directory 261|COPY src/ ./src 262|RUN poetry install --only main 263|``` 264| 265|The two key options we are using here are `--no-root` (skips installing the project source) and `--no-directory` (skips installing any local directory path dependencies, you can omit this if you don't have any). 266|[More information on the options available for `poetry install`]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}). 267| 268| 269|### My requests are timing out! 270| 271|Poetry's default HTTP request timeout is 15 seconds, the same as `pip`. 272|Similar to `PIP_REQUESTS_TIMEOUT`, the **experimental** environment variable `POETRY_REQUESTS_TIMEOUT` 273|can be set to alter this value. 274| 275| 276|### How do I migrate an existing Poetry project using `tool.poetry` section to use the new `project` section (PEP 621)? 277| 278|{{% note %}} 279|Poetry `>=2.0.0` should seamlessly support both `tool.poetry` section only configuration as well using the `project` section. This 280|lets you decide when and if you would like to migrate to using the `project` section as [described by PyPA](https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/pyproject-toml/#declaring-project-metadata-the-project-table). 281| 282|See documentation on [the `pyproject.toml` file]({{< relref "pyproject" >}}), for information specific to Poetry. 283|{{% /note %}} 284| 285|Due to the nature of this change some manual changes to your `pyproject.toml` file is unavoidable in order start using the `project` section. It is multi-platform and the goal is to make it work equally well 22|on Linux, macOS and Windows. 23| 24|## Installation 25| 26|{{% note %}} 27|If you are viewing documentation for the development branch, you may wish to install a preview or development version of Poetry. 28|See the **advanced** installation instructions to use a preview or alternate version of Poetry. 29|{{% /note %}} 30| 31|{{< tabs tabTotal="4" tabID1="installing-with-pipx" tabID2="installing-with-the-official-installer" tabID3="installing-manually" tabID4="ci-recommendations" tabName1="With pipx" tabName2="With the official installer" tabName3="Manually (advanced)" tabName4="CI recommendations">}} 32| 33|{{< tab tabID="installing-with-pipx" >}} 34| 35|[`pipx`](https://github.com/pypa/pipx) is used to install Python CLI applications globally while still isolating them in virtual environments. 36|`pipx` will manage upgrades and uninstalls when used to install Poetry. 37| 38|{{< steps >}} 39|{{< step >}} 40|**Install pipx** 41| 42|If `pipx` is not already installed, you can follow any of the options in the 43|[official pipx installation instructions](https://pipx.pypa.io/stable/how-to/install-pipx.html). 44|Any non-ancient version of `pipx` will do. 45| 46|{{< /step >}} 47|{{< step >}} 48|**Install Poetry** 49| 50|```bash 51|pipx install poetry 52|``` 53|{{< /step >}} 54|{{< step >}} 55|**Install Poetry (advanced)** 56| 57|{{% note %}} 58|You can skip this step, if you simply want the latest version and already installed Poetry as described in the 59|previous step. This step details advanced usages of this installation method. For example, installing Poetry from 60|source, having multiple versions installed at the same time etc. 61|{{% /note %}} 62| 63|`pipx` can install different versions of Poetry, using the same syntax as pip: 64| 65|```bash 66|pipx install poetry==1.8.4 67|``` 68| 69|`pipx` can also install versions of Poetry in parallel, which allows for easy testing of alternate or prerelease 70|versions. Each version is given a unique, user-specified suffix, which will be used to create a unique binary name: 71| 72|```bash 73|pipx install --suffix=@1.8.4 poetry==1.8.4 74|poetry@1.8.4 --version 75|``` 76| 77|```bash 78|pipx install --suffix=@preview --pip-args=--pre poetry 79|poetry@preview --version 80|``` 81| 82|Finally, `pipx` can install any valid [pip requirement spec](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/cli/pip_install/), which 83|allows for installations of the development version from `git`, or even for local testing of pull requests: 84| 85|```bash 86|pipx install --suffix @main git+https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry.git@main 87|pipx install --suffix @pr1234 git+https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry.git@refs/pull/1234/head 88|``` 89| 90|{{< /step >}} 91|{{< step >}} 92|**Update Poetry** 93| 94|```bash 95|pipx upgrade poetry 96|``` 97|{{< /step >}} 98|{{< step >}} 99|**Uninstall Poetry** 100| 101|```bash 102|pipx uninstall poetry 103|``` 104|{{< /step >}} 105|{{< /steps >}} 106| 107|{{< /tab >}} 108|{{< tab tabID="installing-with-the-official-installer" >}} 109| 110|We provide a custom installer that will install Poetry in a new virtual environment 111|and allows Poetry to manage its own environment. 112| 113|{{< steps >}} 114|{{< step >}} 115|**Install Poetry** 116| 117|The installer script is available directly at [install.python-poetry.org](https://install.python-poetry.org), 118|and is developed in [its own repository](https://github.com/python-poetry/install.python-poetry.org). 119|The script can be executed directly (i.e. 'curl python') or downloaded and then executed from disk 120|(e.g. in a CI environment). 121| 122|**Linux, macOS, Windows (WSL)** 123| 124|```bash 125|curl -sSL https://install.python-poetry.org | python3 - Each install method has a different syntax for setting the version that 297|is used in the following examples. 298| 299|**Using pipx** 300| 301|Just as `pipx` is a powerful tool for development use, it is equally useful in a CI environment 302|and should be one of your top choices for use of Poetry in CI. 303| 304|```bash 305|pipx install poetry==2.0.0 306|``` 307| 308|**Using install.python-poetry.org** 309| 310|{{% note %}} 311|The official installer script ([install.python-poetry.org](https://install.python-poetry.org)) offers a streamlined and 312|simplified installation of Poetry, sufficient for developer use or for simple pipelines. For now, it looks like this: 40| 41|```toml 42|[project] 43|name = "poetry-demo" 44|version = "0.1.0" 45|description = "" 46|authors = [ 47| {name = "Sébastien Eustace", email = "sebastien@eustace.io"} 48|] 49|readme = "README.md" 50|requires-python = ">=3.9" 51|dependencies = [ 52|] 53| 54|[build-system] 55|requires = ["poetry-core>=2.0.0,<3.0.0"] 56|build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api" 57|``` 58| 59|Poetry assumes your package contains a package with the same name as `project.name` located in the root of your 60|project. If this is not the case, populate [`tool.poetry.packages`]({{< relref "pyproject#packages" >}}) to specify 61|your packages and their locations. 62| 63|Similarly, the traditional `MANIFEST.in` file is replaced by the `project.readme`, `tool.poetry.include`, and 64|`tool.poetry.exclude` sections. `tool.poetry.exclude` is additionally implicitly populated by your `.gitignore`. For 65|full documentation on the project format, see the [pyproject section]({{< relref "pyproject" >}}) of the documentation. 66| 67|### Setting a Python Version 68| 69|{{% note %}} 70|Unlike with other packages, Poetry will not automatically install a python interpreter for you. 71|If you want to run Python files in your package like a script or application, you must _bring your own_ python interpreter to run them. 72|{{% /note %}} 73| 74|Poetry will require you to explicitly specify what versions of Python you intend to support, and its universal locking 75|will guarantee that your project is installable (and all dependencies claim support for) all supported Python versions. 76|Again, it's important to remember that -- unlike other dependencies -- setting a Python version is merely specifying which versions of Python you intend to support. 77| 78|For example, in this `pyproject.toml` file: 79| 80|```toml 81|[project] 82|requires-python = ">=3.9" 83|``` 84| 85|we are allowing any version of Python 3 that is greater or equal than `3.9.0`. 86| 87|When you run `poetry install`, you must have access to some version of a Python interpreter that satisfies this constraint available on your system. 88|Poetry will not install a Python interpreter for you. 89| 90|### Initialising a pre-existing project 91| 92|Instead of creating a new project, Poetry can be used to 'initialize' a pre-populated 93|directory. To interactively create a `pyproject.toml` file in directory `pre-existing-project`: 94| 95|```bash 96|cd pre-existing-project 97|poetry init 98|``` 99| 100|### Operating modes 101| 102|Poetry can be operated in two different modes. The default mode is the **package mode**, which is the right mode 103|if you want to package your project into an sdist or a wheel and perhaps publish it to a package index. 104|In this mode, some metadata such as `name` and `version`, which are required for packaging, are mandatory. 105|Further, the project itself will be installed in editable mode when running `poetry install`. 106| 107|If you want to use Poetry only for dependency management but not for packaging, you can use the **non-package mode**: 108| 109|```toml 110|[tool.poetry] 111|package-mode = false 112|``` 113| 114|In this mode, metadata such as `name` and `version` are optional. 115|Therefore, it is not possible to build a distribution or publish the project to a package index. 116|Further, when running `poetry install`, Poetry does not try to install the project itself, 117|but only its dependencies (same as `poetry install --no-root`). 118| 119|{{% note %}} 120|In the [pyproject section]({{< relref "pyproject" >}}) you can see which fields are required in package mode. 121|{{% /note %}} 122| 123|### Specifying dependencies 124|If you want to add dependencies to your project, you can specify them in the 125|`project` section. 126| 127|```toml 128|[project] 129|# ... 130|dependencies = [ 131| "pendulum (>=2.1,<3.0)" 132|] 133|``` 134| 135|As you can see, it takes a mapping of **package names** and **version constraints**. 136| 137|Poetry uses this information to search for the right set of files in package "repositories" that you register 138|in the `tool.poetry.source` section, or on [PyPI](https://pypi.org) by default. 139| 140|Also, instead of modifying the `pyproject.toml` file by hand, you can use the `add` command. 141| 142|```bash 143|$ poetry add pendulum 144|``` 145| 146|It will automatically find a suitable version constraint **and install** the package and sub-dependencies. 147| 148|Poetry supports a rich [dependency specification]({{< relref "dependency-specification" >}}) syntax, including caret, 149|tilde, wildcard, inequality and 150|[multiple constraints]({{< relref "dependency-specification#multiple-constraints-dependencies" >}}) requirements. 151| 152|## Using your virtual environment 153| 154|By default, Poetry creates a virtual environment in `{cache-dir}/virtualenvs`. 155|You can change the [`cache-dir`]({{< relref "configuration#cache-dir" >}} "cache-dir configuration documentation") value 156|by editing the Poetry configuration. 157|Additionally, you can use the 158|[`virtualenvs.in-project`]({{< relref "configuration#virtualenvsin-project" >}}) configuration variable to create 159|virtual environments within your project directory. 160| 161|There are several ways to run commands within this virtual environment. 162| 163|{{% note %}} 164|**External virtual environment management** 165| 166|Poetry will detect and respect an existing virtual environment that has been externally activated. This is a powerful 167|mechanism that is intended to be an alternative to Poetry's built-in, simplified environment management. 168| 169|To take advantage of this, simply activate a virtual environment using your preferred method or tooling, before running 170|any Poetry commands that expect to manipulate an environment. 171|{{% /note %}} 172| 173|### Using `poetry run` 174| 175|To run your script simply use `poetry run python your_script.py`. 176|Likewise if you have command line tools such as `pytest` or `black` you can run them using `poetry run pytest`. 177| 178|{{% note %}} 179|If managing your own virtual environment externally, you do not need to use `poetry run` since 180|you will, presumably, already have activated that virtual environment and made available the correct python instance. 181|For example, these commands should output the same python path: 182| 183|```shell 184|conda activate your_env_name 185|which python 186|poetry run which python 187|eval "$(poetry env activate)" 188|which python 189|``` 190| 191|{{% /note %}} 192| 193|### Activating the virtual environment 194| 195|See [Activating the virtual environment]({{< relref "managing-environments#activating-the-environment" >}}). 196| 197|## Version constraints 198| 199|In our example, we are requesting the `pendulum` package with the version constraint `>=2.1.0 <3.0.0`. 200|This means any version greater or equal to 2.1.0 and less than 3.0.0. 201| 202|Please read [Dependency specification]({{< relref "dependency-specification" >}} "Dependency specification documentation") 203|for more in-depth information on versions, how versions relate to each other, and on the different ways you can specify 204|dependencies. 205| 206|{{% note %}} 207|**How does Poetry download the right files?** 208| 209|When you specify a dependency in `pyproject.toml`, Poetry first takes the name of the package 210|that you have requested and searches for it in any repository you have registered using the `repositories` key. 211|If you have not registered any extra repositories, or it does not find a package with that name in the 212|repositories you have specified, it falls back to PyPI. 213| 214|When Poetry finds the right package, it then attempts to find the best match for the version constraint you have 215|specified. 216|{{% /note %}} 217| 218|## Installing dependencies 219| 220|To install the defined dependencies for your project, just run the [`install`]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}) command. 221| 222|```bash 223|poetry install 224|``` 225| 226|When you run this command, one of two things may happen: 227| 228|### Installing without `poetry.lock` 229| 230|If you have never run the command before and there is also no `poetry.lock` file present, 231|Poetry simply resolves all dependencies listed in your `pyproject.toml` file and downloads the latest version of their files. 232| 233|When Poetry has finished installing, it writes all the packages and their exact versions that it downloaded to the `poetry.lock` file, 234|locking the project to those specific versions. 235|You should commit the `poetry.lock` file to your project repo so that all people working on the project are locked to the same versions of dependencies (more below). 236| 237|### Installing with `poetry.lock` 238| 239|This brings us to the second scenario. If there is already a `poetry.lock` file as well as a `pyproject.toml` file 240|when you run `poetry install`, it means either you ran the `install` command before, 241|or someone else on the project ran the `install` command and committed the `poetry.lock` file to the project (which is good). 242| 243|Either way, running `install` when a `poetry.lock` file is present resolves and installs all dependencies that you listed in `pyproject.toml`, 244|but Poetry uses the exact versions listed in `poetry.lock` to ensure that the package versions are consistent for everyone working on your project. 245|As a result you will have all dependencies requested by your `pyproject.toml` file, 246|but they may not all be at the very latest available versions 247|(some dependencies listed in the `poetry.lock` file may have released newer versions since the file was created). 248|This is by design, it ensures that your project does not break because of unexpected changes in dependencies. 249| 250|### Committing your `poetry.lock` file to version control 251| 252|#### As an application developer 253| 254|Application developers commit `poetry.lock` to get more reproducible builds. 255| 256|Committing this file to VC is important because it will cause anyone who sets up the project 257|to use the exact same versions of the dependencies that you are using. 258|Your CI server, production machines, other developers in your team, 259|everything and everyone runs on the same dependencies, 260|which mitigates the potential for bugs affecting only some parts of the deployments. 261|Even if you develop alone, in six months when reinstalling the project you can feel confident 262|the dependencies installed are still working even if your dependencies released many new versions since then. 263|(See note below about using the update command.) 264| 265|{{% warning %}} If you have added the recommended [`[build-system]`]({{< relref "pyproject#poetry-and-pep-517" >}}) section to your project's pyproject.toml then you _can_ successfully install your project and its dependencies into a virtual environment using a command like `pip install -e .`. However, pip will not use the lock file to determine dependency versions as the poetry-core build system is intended for library developers (see next section). 266|{{% /warning %}} 267| 268|#### As a library developer 269| 270|Library developers have more to consider. Your users are application developers, and your library will run in a Python environment you don't control. 271| 272|The application ignores your library's lock file. It can use whatever dependency version meets the constraints in your `pyproject.toml`. The application will probably use the latest compatible dependency version. If your library's `poetry.lock` falls behind some new dependency version that breaks things for your users, you're likely to be the last to find out about it. 273| 274|A simple way to avoid such a scenario is to omit the `poetry.lock` file. However, by doing so, you sacrifice reproducibility and performance to a certain extent. Without a lockfile, it can be difficult to find the reason for failing tests, because in addition to obvious code changes an unnoticed library update might be the culprit. Further, Poetry will have to lock before installing a dependency if `poetry.lock` has been omitted. Depending on the number of dependencies, locking may take a significant amount of time. 275| 276|If you do not want to give up the reproducibility and performance benefits, consider a regular refresh of `poetry.lock` to stay up-to-date and reduce the risk of sudden breakage for users. 277| 278|### Installing dependencies only 279| 280|The current project is installed in [editable](https://pip.pypa.io/en/stable/topics/local-project-installs/) mode by default. 281| 282|If you want to install the dependencies only, run the `install` command with the `--no-root` flag: 283| 284|```bash 285|poetry install --no-root 286|``` 287| 288|## Updating dependencies to their latest versions 289| 290|As mentioned above, the `poetry.lock` file prevents you from automatically getting the latest versions 291|of your dependencies. 292|To update to the latest versions, use the `update` command. 293|This will fetch the latest matching versions (according to your `pyproject.toml` file) 294|and update the lock file with the new versions. 295|(This is equivalent to deleting the `poetry.lock` file and running `install` again.) 296| 297|{{% note %}} 298|Poetry will display a **Warning** when executing an install command if `poetry.lock` and `pyproject.toml` 299|are not synchronized. 300|{{% /note %}} --- END FILE: docs/basic-usage.md --- --- FILE: These are mostly guidelines, not rules. Use 19|your best judgement, and feel free to propose changes to this document in a pull request. 20| 21|## How to contribute 22| 23|### Reporting bugs 24| 25|This section guides you through submitting a bug report for Poetry. 26|Following these guidelines helps maintainers and the community understands your report, reproduces the behavior, and finds 27|related reports. 28| 29|#### Before submitting a bug report 30| 31|* **Check the [FAQ]** for a list of common questions and problems. 32|* **Check the [blog]** for release notes from recent releases, including steps for upgrading and known issues. 33|* **Check that your issue does not already exist** in the [issue tracker]. 34|* **Make sure your issue is really a bug, and is not a support request or question** better suited for [Discussions] 35|or [Discord]. 36|* **Try running your commands with the** `--no-cache` **flag**. 37|* **Try clearing your cache with** `poetry cache clear --all PyPI` **and rerunning your commands**. 38| 39|{{% note %}} 40|If you find a **Closed** issue that seems like it is the same thing that you're experiencing, open a new issue and 41|include a link to the original issue in the body of your new one. 42|{{% /note %}} 43| 44|#### How do I submit a bug report? 45| 46|Bugs concerning Poetry and poetry-core should be submitted to the main [issue tracker], using the correct 47|[issue template]. 48| 49|Explain the problem and make it easy for others to search for and understand: 50| 51|* **Use a clear and descriptive title** for the issue to identify the problem. 52|* **Describe the exact steps which reproduce the problem** in as many details as possible. 53|* **Describe the behavior you observed after following the steps** and point out how this is a bug. 54|* **Explain which behavior you expected to see instead and why.** 55|* **If the problem involves an unexpected error being raised**, execute the problematic command in **debug** mode 56|(with `-vvv` flag). 57| 58|Provide detailed steps for reproduction of your issue: 59| 60|* **Provide your pyproject.toml file** in a [Gist](https://gist.github.com), pastebin, or example repository after 61|removing potential private information like private package repositories or names. 62|* **Provide specific examples to demonstrate the steps to reproduce the issue**. This could be an example repository, a 63|sequence of steps run in a container, or just a pyproject.toml for very simple cases. 64|* **Are you unable to reliably reproduce the issue?** If so, provide details about how often the problem happens 65|and under which conditions it normally happens. 66| 67|Provide more context by answering these questions: 68| 69|* **Did the problem start happening recently** (e.g., after updating to a new version of Poetry) or was this always a 70|problem? 71|* If the problem started happening recently, **can you reproduce the problem in an older version of Poetry?** What's the 72|most recent version in which the problem does not happen? 73|* **Is there anything exotic or unusual about your environment?** This could include use of special container images, 74|newer CPU architectures like Apple Silicon, or corporate proxies that intercept or modify your network traffic. 75| 76|Include details about your configuration and environment: 77| 78|* **Which version of Poetry are you using?** You can get the exact version by running `poetry --version`. 79|* **What version of Python is being used to run Poetry?** Execute the `poetry debug info` to get this information. 80|* **What's the name and version of the OS you're using?** Examples include Ubuntu 22.04 or macOS 12.6. 81| 82|To give others the best chance to understand and reproduce your issue, please be sure to put extra effort into your 83|reproduction steps. You can both rule out local configuration issues on your end, and ensure others can cleanly 84|reproduce your issue if attempt all reproductions in a pristine container (or VM), and provide the steps you performed 85|inside that container/VM in your issue report. 86| 87|### Suggesting enhancements 88| 89|This section guides you through submitting an enhancement suggestion for Poetry, including completely new features as 90|well as improvements to existing functionality. Following these guidelines helps maintainers and the community 91|understand your suggestion and find related suggestions. 92| 93|#### Before submitting a suggested enhancement 94| 95|* **Check the [FAQ]** for a list of common questions and problems. 96|* **Check that your issue does not already exist** in the [issue tracker]. 97| 98|#### How do I submit a suggested enhancement? 99| 100|Suggested enhancements concerning Poetry and poetry-core should be submitted to the main [issue tracker], using the 101|correct [issue template]. 102| 103|* **Use a clear and descriptive title** for the issue to identify the suggestion. 104|* **Provide a detailed description of the proposed enhancement**, with specific steps or examples when possible. 105|* **Describe the current behavior** and **explain which behavior you would like to see instead**, and why. 106| 107|### Documentation contributions 108| 109|One of the simplest ways to get started contributing to a project is through improving documentation. Poetry is 110|constantly evolving, and this means that sometimes our documentation has gaps. You can help by adding missing sections, 111|editing the existing content to be more accessible, or creating new content such as tutorials, FAQs, etc. 112| 113|{{% note %}} 114|GitHub [Discussions](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/discussions) and the 115|[kind/question label](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/labels/kind%2Fquestion) are excellent sources for FAQ 116|candidates. 117|{{% /note %}} 118| 119|Issues pertaining to the documentation are usually marked with the [area/docs label], which will also trigger a preview 120|of the changes as rendered by this website. 121| 122|### Code contributions 123| 124|#### Picking an issue 125| 126|{{% note %}} 127|If you are a first time contributor, and are looking for an issue to take on, you might want to look for 128|at the [contributing page](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/contribute) for candidates. We do our best to curate 129|good issues for first-time contributors there, but do fall behind -- so if you don't see anything good, feel free to 130|ask. 131|{{% /note %}} 132| 133|If you would like to take on an issue, feel free to comment on the issue tagging `@python-poetry/triage`. 134|We are more than happy to discuss solutions on the issue. If you would like help with navigating the code base, are 135|looking for something to work on, or want feedback on a design or change, join us on our [Discord server][Discord] or 136|start a [Discussion][Discussions]. 137| 138|#### Local development 139| 140|Poetry is developed using Poetry. Refer to the [documentation] to install Poetry in your local environment. 141| 142|{{% note %}} 143|Poetry's development toolchain requires Python 3.11 or newer. 144|{{% /note %}} 145| 146|You should first fork the Poetry repository and then clone it locally, so that you can make pull requests against the 147|project. If you are new to Git and pull request-based development, GitHub provides a 148|[guide](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/quickstart/contributing-to-projects) you will find helpful. 149| 150|Next, you should install Poetry's dependencies, and run the test suite to make sure everything is working as expected: 151| 152|```bash 153|poetry install 154|poetry run pytest 155|``` 156| 157|{{% note %}} 158|If you want to see the coverage stats after the tests are complete, use: 159| 160|```bash 161|poetry run pytest --cov=src/poetry --cov-report term 162|``` 163|{{% /note %}} 164| 165|When you contribute to Poetry, automated tools will be run to make sure your code is suitable to be merged. Besides 166|pytest, you will need to make sure your code typechecks properly using [mypy](https://mypy-lang.org/): 167| 168|```bash 169|poetry run mypy 170|``` 171| 172|Finally, a great deal of linting tools are run on your code, to try and ensure consistent code style and root out common 173|mistakes. The [pre-commit](https://pre-commit.com/) tool is used to install and run these tools, and requires one-time 174|setup: 175| 176|```bash 177|poetry run pre-commit install 178|``` 179| 180|pre-commit will now run and check your code every time you make a commit. By default, it will only run on changed files, 181|but you can run it on all files manually (this may be useful if you altered the pre-commit config): 182| 183|```bash 184|poetry run pre-commit run --all-files 185|``` 186| 187|#### Pull requests 188| 189|* Fill out the pull request body completely and describe your changes as accurately as possible. The pull request body 190|should be kept up to date as it will usually form the base for the final merge commit and the changelog entry. 191|* Be sure that your pull request contains tests that cover the changed or added code. Tests are generally required for 192|code be to be considered mergeable, and code without passing tests will not be merged. 193|* Ensure your pull request passes the mypy and pre-commit checks. Remember that you can run these tools locally 194|instead of relying on remote CI. 195|* If your changes warrant a documentation change, the pull request must also update the documentation. Make sure to 196|review the documentation preview generated by CI for any rendering issues. 197| 198|{{% note %}} 199|Make sure your branch is [rebased](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/using-git/about-git-rebase) against the latest 200|base branch. A maintainer might ask you to ensure the branch is up-to-date prior to merging your pull request 201|(especially if there have been CI changes on the base branch), and will also ask you to fix any conflicts. 202|{{% /note %}} 203| 204|All pull requests, unless otherwise instructed, need to be first accepted into the `main` branch. Maintainers will 205|generally decide if any backports to other branches are required, and carry them out as needed. 206| 207|### Issue triage 208| 209|{{% note %}} 210|If you have an issue that hasn't had any attention, you can ping us `@python-poetry/triage` on the issue. Please give us 211|reasonable time to get to your issue first, and avoid pinging any individuals directly, especially if they are not part 212|of the Poetry team. 213|{{% /note %}} 214| 215|If you are helping with the triage of reported issues, this section provides some useful information to assist you in 216|your contribution. 217| 218|#### Triage steps 219| 220|1. Determine what area and versions of Poetry the issue is related to, and set the appropriate labels (e.g. 221|`version/x.x.x`, `area/docs`, `area/venv`), and remove the `status/triage` label. 222|2. If requested information (such as debug logs, pyproject.toml, etc.) is not provided and is relevant, request it from 223|the author. 224| 1. Set the `status/waiting-on-response` label while waiting to hear back from the author. 225|3. Attempt to reproduce the issue with the reported Poetry version or request further clarification from the author. 226|4. Ensure the issue is not already resolved. Try reproducing it on the latest stable release, the latest prerelease (if 227|present), and the development branch. 228|5. If the issue cannot be reproduced, 229| 1. request more reproduction steps and clarification from the issue's author, 230| 2. set the `status/needs-reproduction` label, 231| 3. close the issue if there is no reproduction forthcoming. 232|6. If the issue can be reproduced, 233| 1. comment on the issue confirming so, 234| 2. set the `status/confirmed` label, 235| 3. if possible, identify the root cause of the issue, 236| 4. if interested, You can participate in the discussions about stabilizing this feature 17|[here](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry/issues/2740). 18| 19|And as always, your contributions towards the goal of improving this feature are also welcome. 20|{{% /warning %}} 21| 22|Poetry allows a project developer to introduce support for, build and distribute native extensions within their project. 23|In order to achieve this, at the highest level, the following steps are required. 24| 25|{{< steps >}} 26|{{< step >}} 27|**Add Build Dependencies** 28| 29|The build dependencies, in this context, refer to those Python packages that are required in order to successfully execute 30|your build script. Common examples include `cython`, `meson`, `maturin`, `setuptools` etc., depending on how your 31|extension is built. 32| 33|{{% note %}} 34|You must assume that only Python built-ins are available by default in a build environment. This means, if you need 35|even packages like `setuptools`, it must be explicitly declared. 36|{{% /note %}} 37| 38|The necessary build dependencies must be added to the `build-system.requires` section of your `pyproject.toml` file. 39| 40|```toml 41|[build-system] 42|requires = ["poetry-core", "setuptools", "cython"] 43|build-backend = "poetry.core.masonry.api" 44|``` 45| 46|{{% note %}} 47|It is recommended that you consider specifying version constraints to all entries in `build-system.requires` in order to 48|avoid surprises if one of the packages introduce a breaking change. For example, you can set `cython` to 49|`cython>=3.0.11,<4.0.0` to ensure no major version upgrades are used. 50|{{% /note %}} 51| 52|{{% note %}} 53|If you wish to develop the build script within your project's virtual environment, then you must also add the 54|dependencies to your project explicitly to a dependency group - the name of which is not important. 55| 56|```sh 57|poetry add --group=build setuptools cython 58|``` 59|{{% /note %}} 60| 61|{{< /step >}} 62| 63|{{< step >}} 64|**Add Build Script** 65| 66|The build script can be a free-form Python script that uses any dependency specified in the previous step. This can be 67|named as needed, but **must** be located within the project root directory (or a subdirectory) and also **must** 68|be included in your source distribution. You can see the [example snippets section]({{< relref "#example-snippets" >}}) 69|for inspiration. 70| 71|{{% note %}} 72|The build script is always executed from the project root. And it is expected to move files around to their destinations 73|as expected by Poetry as per your `pyproject.toml` file. 74|{{% /note %}} 75| 76|```toml 77|[tool.poetry.build] 78|script = "relative/path/to/build-extension.py" 79|``` 80| 81|{{% note %}} 82|The name of the build script is arbitrary. Common practice has been to name it `build.py`, however, this is not 83|mandatory. You **should** consider [using a subdirectory]({{< relref "#can-i-store-the-build-script-in-a-subdirectory" >}}) 84|if feasible. 85|{{% /note %}} 86| 87|{{< /step >}} 88| 89|{{< step >}} 90|**Specify Distribution Files** 91| 92|{{% warning %}} 93|The following is an example, and should not be considered as complete. 94|{{% /warning %}} 95| 96|```toml 97|[tool.poetry] 98|... 99|include = [ 100| { path = "package/**/*.so", format = "wheel" }, 101| # sources must be present in sdist, can be ignored if you only have *.pyx sources 102| { path = "package/**/*.c", format = "sdist" }, 103|] 104|``` 105| 106|The key takeaway here should be the following. You can refer to the [`pyproject.toml`]({{< relref "pyproject#exclude-and-include" >}}) 107|documentation for information on each of the relevant sections. 108| 109|1. Include your build outputs in your wheel. 110|2. Exclude your build inputs from your wheel. 111|3. Include your build inputs to your source distribution. 112| 113|{{< /step >}} 114| 115|{{< /steps >}} 116| 117|## Example Snippets 118| 119|### Cython 120| 121|{{< tabs tabTotal="3" When `poetry install` is run, it is executed prior to installing the project's root package. 350|2. When `poetry build` is run, it is executed prior to building distributions. 351|3. 6| 7|menu: 8| docs: 9| weight: 80 10|--- 11| 12|# Plugins 13| 14|Poetry supports using and building plugins if you wish to 15|alter or expand Poetry's functionality with your own. 16| 17|For example if your environment poses special requirements 18|on the behaviour of Poetry which do not apply to the majority of its users 19|or if you wish to accomplish something with Poetry in a way that is not desired by most users. 20| 21|In these cases you could consider creating a plugin to handle your specific logic. 22| 23| 24|## Creating a plugin 25| 26|A plugin is a regular Python package which ships its code as part of the package 27|and may also depend on further packages. 28| 29|### Plugin package 30| 31|The plugin package must depend on Poetry 32|and declare a proper [plugin]({{< relref "pyproject#plugins" >}}) in the `pyproject.toml` file. 33| 34|```toml 35|[project] 36|name = "my-poetry-plugin" 37|version = "1.0.0" 38|# ... 39|requires-python = ">=3.7" 40|dependencies = [ 41| "poetry (>=1.2,<2.0)", 42|] 43| 44|[project.entry-points."poetry.plugin"] 45|demo = "poetry_demo_plugin.plugin:MyPlugin" 46|``` 47| 48|### Generic plugins 49| 50|Every plugin has to supply a class which implements the `poetry.plugins.Plugin` interface. 51| 52|The `activate()` method of the plugin is called after the plugin is loaded 53|and receives an instance of `Poetry` as well as an instance of `cleo.io.io.IO`. 54| 55|Using these two objects all configuration can be read 56|and all public internal objects and state can be manipulated as desired. 57| 58|Example: 59| 60|```python 61|from cleo.io.io import IO 62| 63|from poetry.plugins.plugin import Plugin 64|from poetry.poetry import Poetry 65| 66| 67|class MyPlugin(Plugin): 68| 69| def activate(self, poetry: Poetry, io: IO): 70| io.write_line("Setting readme") 71| poetry.package.readme = "README.md" 72| ... 73|``` 74| 75|### Application plugins 76| 77|If you want to add commands or options to the `poetry` script you need 78|to create an application plugin which implements the `poetry.plugins.ApplicationPlugin` interface. 79| 80|The `activate()` method of the application plugin is called after the plugin is loaded 81|and receives an instance of `poetry.console.Application`. 82| 83|```python 84|from cleo.commands.command import Command 85|from poetry.plugins.application_plugin import ApplicationPlugin 86| 87| 88|class CustomCommand(Command): 89| 90| name = "my-command" 91| 92| def handle(self) -> int: 93| self.line("My command") 94| 95| return 0 96| 97| 98|def factory(): 99| return CustomCommand() 100| 101| 102|class MyApplicationPlugin(ApplicationPlugin): 103| def activate(self, application): 104| application.command_loader.register_factory("my-command", factory) 105|``` 106| 107|{{% note %}} 108|It's possible to do the following to register the command: 109| 110|```python 111|application.add(MyCommand()) 112|``` 113| 114|However, it is **strongly** recommended to register a new factory 115|in the command loader to defer the loading of the command when it's actually 116|called. 117| 118|This will help keep the performances of Poetry good. 119|{{% /note %}} 120| 121|The plugin also must be declared in the `pyproject.toml` file of the plugin package 122|as a `poetry.application.plugin` plugin: 123| 124|```toml 125|[tool.poetry.plugins."poetry.application.plugin"] 126|foo-command = "poetry_demo_plugin.plugin:MyApplicationPlugin" 127|``` 128| 129|{{% warning %}} 130|A plugin **must not** remove or modify in any way the core commands of Poetry. 131|{{% /warning %}} 132| 133| 134|### Event handler 135| 136|Plugins can also listen to specific events and act on them if necessary. 137| 138|These events are fired by [Cleo](https://github.com/python-poetry/cleo) 139|and are accessible from the `cleo.events.console_events` module. 140| 141|- `COMMAND`: this event allows attaching listeners before any command is executed. 142|- `SIGNAL`: this event allows some actions to be performed after the command execution is interrupted. 143|- `TERMINATE`: this event allows listeners to be attached after the command. 144|- `ERROR`: this event occurs when an uncaught exception is raised. 145| 146|Let's see how to implement an application event handler. For this example 147|we will see how to load environment variables from a `.env` file before executing 148|a command. 149| 150| 151|```python 152|from cleo.events.console_events import COMMAND 153|from cleo.events.console_command_event import ConsoleCommandEvent 154|from cleo.events.event_dispatcher import EventDispatcher 155|from dotenv import load_dotenv 156|from poetry.console.application import Application 157|from poetry.console.commands.env_command import EnvCommand 158|from poetry.plugins.application_plugin import ApplicationPlugin 159| 160| 161|class MyApplicationPlugin(ApplicationPlugin): 162| def activate(self, application: Application): 163| application.event_dispatcher.add_listener( 164| COMMAND, self.load_dotenv 165| ) 166| 167| def load_dotenv( 168| self, 169| event: ConsoleCommandEvent, 170| event_name: str, 171| dispatcher: EventDispatcher 172| ) -> None: 173| command = event.command 174| if not isinstance(command, EnvCommand): 175| return 176| 177| io = event.io 178| 179| if io.is_debug(): 180| io.write_line( 181| "Loading environment variables." 182| ) 183| 184| load_dotenv() 185|``` 186| 187| 188|## Using plugins 189| 190|Installed plugin packages are automatically loaded when Poetry starts up. 191| 192|You have multiple ways to install plugins for Poetry 193| 194|### With `pipx inject` 195| 196|If you used `pipx` to install Poetry you can add the plugin packages via the `pipx inject` command. 197| 198|```shell 199|pipx inject poetry poetry-plugin 200|``` 201| 202|If you want to uninstall a plugin, you can run: 203| 204|```shell 205|pipx uninject poetry poetry-plugin # For pipx versions >= 1.2.0 206| 207|pipx runpip poetry uninstall poetry-plugin # For pipx versions < 1.2.0 208|``` 209| 210|### With `pip` 211| 212|The `pip` binary in Poetry's virtual environment can also be used to install and remove plugins. 213|The environment variable `$POETRY_HOME` here is used to represent the path to the virtual environment. 214|The [installation instructions](/docs/) can be referenced if you are not 215|sure where Poetry has been installed. 216| 217|To add a plugin, you can use `pip install`: 218| 219|```shell 220|$POETRY_HOME/bin/pip install --user poetry-plugin 221|``` 222| 223|If you want to uninstall a plugin, you can run: 224| 225|```shell 226|$POETRY_HOME/bin/pip uninstall poetry-plugin 227|``` 228| 229|### The `self add` command 230| 231|{{% warning %}} 232|Especially on Windows, `self add` and `self remove` may be problematic 233|so that other methods should be preferred. 234|{{% /warning %}} 235| 236|```bash 237|poetry self add poetry-plugin 238|``` 239| 240|The `self add` command will ensure that the plugin is compatible with the current version of Poetry 241|and install the needed packages for the plugin to work. 242| 243|The package specification formats supported by the `self add` command are the same as the ones supported 244|by the [`add` command]({{< relref "cli#add" >}}). 245| 246|If you no longer need a plugin and want to uninstall it, you can use the `self remove` command. 247| 248|```shell 249|poetry self remove poetry-plugin 250|``` 251| 252|You can also list all currently installed plugins by running: 253| 254|```shell 255|poetry self show plugins 256|``` 257| 258|### Project plugins 259| 260|You can also specify that a plugin is required for your project 261|in the `tool.poetry.requires-plugins` section of the pyproject.toml file: 262| 263|```toml 264|[tool.poetry.requires-plugins] 265|my-application-plugin = ">1.0" 266|custom-plugin = {path = "custom_plugin", develop = true} 267|``` 268| 269|If the plugin is not installed in Poetry's own environment when running `poetry install`, 270|it will be installed only for the current project under `.poetry/plugins` 271|in the project's directory. 272| 273|The syntax to specify `plugins` is the same as for [dependencies]({{< relref "managing-dependencies" >}}). 274|Plugins can be installed in editable mode using path dependencies with `develop = true`, 275|which is useful for plugin development. 276| 277|{{% warning %}} 278|You can even overwrite a plugin in Poetry's own environment with another version. 279|However, if a plugin's dependencies are not compatible with packages in Poetry's own 280|environment, installation will fail. 281|{{% /warning %}} 282| 283| 284|## Maintaining a plugin 285| 286|When writing a plugin, you will probably access internals of Poetry, since there is no 287|stable public API. Although we try our best to deprecate methods first, before 288|removing them, sometimes the signature of an internal method has to be changed. 289| 290|As the author of a plugin, you are probably testing your plugin 291|against the latest release of Poetry. 292|Additionally, you should consider testing against the latest release branch and the 293|main branch of Poetry and schedule a CI job that runs regularly even if you did not 294|make any changes to your plugin. 295|This way, you will notice internal changes that break your plugin immediately 296|and can prepare for the next Poetry For legacy reasons and to define additional information that are only used by Poetry 16|the [`tool.poetry.dependencies`]({{< relref "pyproject#dependencies-and-dependency-groups" >}}) sections can be used. 17| 18|See [Dependency specification]({{< relref "dependency-specification" >}}) for more information. 19| 20|## Dependency groups 21| 22|Poetry provides a way to **organize** your dependencies by **groups**. 23| 24|The dependencies declared in `project.dependencies` respectively `tool.poetry.dependencies` 25|are part of an implicit `main` group. Those dependencies are required by your project during runtime. 26| 27|Besides the `main` dependencies, you might have dependencies that are only needed to test your project 28|or to build the documentation. 29| 30|To declare a new dependency group, use a `dependency-groups` section according to PEP 735 or 31|a `tool.poetry.group.` section where `` is the name of your dependency group (for instance, `test`): 32| 33|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="group-pep735" tabID2="group-poetry" tabName1="[dependency-groups]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 34| 35|{{< tab tabID="group-pep735" >}} 36|```toml 37|[dependency-groups] 38|test = [ 39| "pytest (>=6.0.0,<7.0.0)", 40| "pytest-mock", 41|] 42|``` 43|{{< /tab >}} 44| 45|{{< tab tabID="group-poetry" >}} 46|```toml 47|[tool.poetry.group.test.dependencies] 48|pytest = "^6.0.0" 49|pytest-mock = "*" 50|``` 51|{{< /tab >}} 52|{{< /tabs >}} 53| 54| 55|{{% note %}} 56|All dependencies **must be compatible with each other** across groups since they will 57|be resolved regardless of whether they are required for installation or not (see [Installing group dependencies]({{< relref "#installing-group-dependencies" >}})). 58| 59|Think of dependency groups as **labels** associated with your dependencies: they don't have any bearings 60|on whether their dependencies will be resolved and installed **by default**, they are simply a way to organize 61|the dependencies logically. 62|{{% /note %}} 63| 64|{{% note %}} 65|Dependency groups, other than the implicit `main` group, 66|must only contain dependencies you need in your development process. 67|To declare a set of dependencies, which add additional functionality to the project 68|during runtime, use [extras]({{< relref "pyproject#extras" >}}) instead. 69|{{% /note %}} 70| 71| 72|### Optional groups 73| 74|A dependency group can be declared as optional. This makes sense when you have 75|a group of dependencies that are only required in a particular environment or for 76|a specific purpose. 77| 78|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="group-optional-pep735" tabID2="group-optional-poetry" tabName1="[dependency-groups]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 79| 80|{{< tab tabID="group-optional-pep735" >}} 81|```toml 82|[dependency-groups] 83|docs = [ 84| "mkdocs", 85|] 86| 87|[tool.poetry.group.docs] 88|optional = true 89|``` 90|{{< /tab >}} 91| 92|{{< tab tabID="group-optional-poetry" >}} 93|```toml 94|[tool.poetry.group.docs] 95|optional = true 96| 97|[tool.poetry.group.docs.dependencies] 98|mkdocs = "*" 99|``` 100|{{< /tab >}} 101|{{< /tabs >}} 102| 103| 104| 105|Optional groups can be installed in addition to the **default** dependencies by using the `--with` 106|option of the [`install`]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}) command. 107| 108|```bash 109|poetry install --with docs 110|``` 111| 112|{{% warning %}} 113|Optional group dependencies will **still** be resolved alongside other dependencies, so 114|special care should be taken to ensure they are compatible with each other. 115|{{% /warning %}} 116| 117|### Including dependencies from other groups 118| 119|You can include dependencies from one group in another group. 120|This is useful when you want to aggregate dependencies from multiple groups into a single group. 121| 122|{{< tabs tabTotal="2" tabID1="group-include-pep735" tabID2="group-include-poetry" tabName1="[dependency-groups]" tabName2="[tool.poetry]">}} 123| 124|{{< tab tabID="group-include-pep735" >}} 125|```toml 126|[dependency-groups] 127|test = [ 128| "pytest (>=8.0.0,<9.0.0)", 129|] 130|lint = [ 131| "ruff (>=0.11.0,<0.12.0)", 132|] 133|dev = [ 134| { include-group = "test" }, 135| { include-group = "lint" }, 136| "tox", 137|] 138|``` 139|{{< /tab >}} 140| 141|{{< tab tabID="group-include-poetry" >}} 142|```toml 143|[tool.poetry.group.test.dependencies] 144|pytest = "^8.0.0" 145| 146|[tool.poetry.group.lint.dependencies] 147|ruff = "^0.11" 148| 149|[tool.poetry.group.dev] 150|include-groups = [ 151| "test", 152| "lint", 153|] 154| 155|[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies] 156|tox = "*" 157|``` 158|{{< /tab >}} 159|{{< /tabs >}} 160| 161|In this example, the `dev` group includes all dependencies from the `test` and `lint` groups. 162| 163|### Adding a dependency to a group 164| 165|The [`add`]({{< relref "cli#add" >}}) command is the preferred way to add dependencies 166|to a group. This is done by using the `--group (-G)` option. 167| 168|```bash 169|poetry add pytest --group test 170|``` 171| 172|If the group does not already exist, it will be created automatically. 173| 174|### Installing group dependencies 175| 176|**By default**, dependencies across **all non-optional groups** will be installed when executing 177|`poetry install`. 178| 179|{{% note %}} 180|The default set of dependencies for a project includes the implicit `main` group as well as all 181|groups that are not explicitly marked as an [optional group]({{< relref "#optional-groups" >}}). 182|{{% /note %}} 183| 184|You can **exclude** one or more groups with the `--without` option: 185| 186|```bash 187|poetry install --without test,docs 188|``` 189| 190|You can also opt in [optional groups]({{< relref "#optional-groups" >}}) by using the `--with` option: 191| 192|```bash 193|poetry install --with docs 194|``` 195| 196|{{% warning %}} 197|When used together, `--without` takes precedence over `--with`. For example, the following command 198|will only install the dependencies specified in the optional `test` group. 199| 200|```bash 201|poetry install --with test,docs --without docs 202|``` 203|{{% /warning %}} 204| 205|Finally, in some case you might want to install **only specific groups** of dependencies 206|without installing the default set of dependencies. For that purpose, you can use 207|the `--only` option. 208| 209|```bash 210|poetry install --only docs 211|``` 212| 213|{{% note %}} 214|If you only want to install the project's runtime dependencies, you can do so with the 215|`--only main` notation: 216| 217|```bash 218|poetry install --only main 219|``` 220|{{% /note %}} 221| 222|{{% note %}} 223|If you want to install the project root, and no other dependencies, you can use 224|the `--only-root` option. 225| 226|```bash 227|poetry install --only-root 228|``` 229|{{% /note %}} 230| 231|### Removing dependencies from a group 232| 233|The [`remove`]({{< relref "cli#remove" >}}) command supports a `--group` option 234|to remove packages from a specific group: 235| 236|```bash 237|poetry remove mkdocs --group docs 238|``` 239| 240|## Synchronizing dependencies 241| 242|Poetry supports what's called dependency synchronization. Dependency synchronization ensures 243|that the locked dependencies in the `poetry.lock` file are the only ones present 244|in the environment, removing anything that's not necessary. 245| 246|This is done by using the `sync` command: 247| 248|```bash 249|poetry sync 250|``` 251| 252|The `sync` command can be combined with any [dependency groups]({{< relref "#dependency-groups" >}}) related options 253|to synchronize the environment with specific groups. Note that extras are separate. 254|Any extras not selected for install are always removed. 255| 256|```bash 257|poetry sync --without dev 258|poetry sync --with docs 259|poetry sync --only dev 260|``` 261| 262|## Layering optional groups 263| 264|When using the `install` command without the `--sync` option, you can install any subset of optional groups without removing 265|those that are already installed. This is very useful, for example, in multi-stage 266|Docker builds, where you run `poetry install` multiple times in different build stages. --- END FILE: docs/managing-dependencies.md --- --- FILE: You must fully specify all arguments for 24|your hook if you make use of `args:`. 25|{{% /note %}} 26| 27|{{% note %}} 28|If the `pyproject.toml` file is not in the root directory, you can specify `args: ["-C", "./subdirectory"]`. 29|{{% /note %}} 30| 31|## poetry-check 32| 33|The `poetry-check` hook calls the `poetry check` command 34|to make sure the poetry configuration does not get committed in a broken state. 35| 36|### Arguments 37| 38|The hook takes the same arguments as the poetry command. 39|For more information see the [check command]({{< relref "cli#check" >}}). 40| 41|## poetry-lock 42| 43|The `poetry-lock` hook calls the `poetry lock` command 44|to make sure the lock file is up-to-date when committing changes. 45| 46|### Arguments 47| 48|The hook takes the same arguments as the poetry command. 49|For more information see the [lock command]({{< relref "cli#lock" >}}). 50| 51|## poetry-export 52| 53|The `poetry-export` hook calls the `poetry export` command 54|to sync your `requirements.txt` file with your current dependencies. 55| 56|{{% warning %}} 57|This hook is provided by the [Export Poetry Plugin](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry-plugin-export). 58|{{% /warning %}} 59| 60|{{% note %}} 61|It is recommended to run the [`poetry-lock`](#poetry-lock) hook or [`poetry-check`](#poetry-check) with argument `--lock` prior to this one. 62|{{% /note %}} 63| 64|### Arguments 65| 66|The hook takes the same arguments as the poetry command. 67|For more information, see the [export command]({{< relref "cli#export" >}}). 68| 69|The default arguments are `args: ["-f", "requirements.txt", "-o", "requirements.txt"]`, 70|which will create/update the `requirements.txt` file in the current working directory. 71| 72|You may add `verbose: true` in your `.pre-commit-config.yaml` in order to output to the 73|console: 74| 75|```yaml 76|hooks: 77|- id: poetry-export 78| args: ["-f", "requirements.txt"] 79| verbose: true 80|``` 81| 82|Also, `--dev` can be added to `args` to write dev-dependencies to `requirements.txt`: 83| 84|```yaml 85|hooks: 86|- id: poetry-export 87| args: ["--dev", "-f", "requirements.txt", "-o", "requirements.txt"] 88|``` 89| 90|## poetry-install 91| 92|The `poetry-install` hook calls the `poetry install` command to make sure all locked packages are installed. 93|In order to install this hook, you either need to specify `default_install_hook_types`, or you have 94|to install it via `pre-commit install --install-hooks -t post-checkout -t post-merge`. 95| 96|### Arguments 97| 98|The hook takes the same arguments as the poetry command. 99|For more information, see the [install command]({{< relref "cli#install" >}}). 100| 101|## Usage 102| 103|For more information on how to use pre-commit, please see the [official documentation](https://pre-commit.com/). 104| 105|A minimalistic `.pre-commit-config.yaml` example: 106| 107|```yaml 108|repos: 109|- repo: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry 110| rev: '' # add version here 111| hooks: 112| - id: poetry-check 113| - id: poetry-lock 114| - id: poetry-export 115| - id: poetry-install 116|``` 117| 118|A `.pre-commit-config.yaml` example for a monorepo setup or if the `pyproject.toml` file is not in the root directory: 119| 120|```yaml 121|repos: 122|- repo: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry 123| rev: '' # add version here 124| hooks: 125| - id: poetry-check 126| args: ["-C", "./subdirectory"] 127| - id: poetry-lock 128| args: ["-C", "./subdirectory"] 129| - id: poetry-export 130| args: ["-C", "./subdirectory", "-f", "requirements.txt", "-o", "./subdirectory/requirements.txt"] 131| - id: poetry-install 132| args: ["-C", "./subdirectory"] 133|``` 134| 135|## FAQ 136| 137|### Why does `pre-commit autoupdate` not update to the latest version? 138| 139|`pre-commit autoupdate` updates the `rev` for each repository defined in your `.pre-commit-config.yaml` 140|to the latest available tag in the default branch. 141| 142|Poetry follows a branching strategy where the default branch is the active development branch, 143|and fixes get backported to stable branches. New tags are assigned in these stable branches. 144| 145|`pre-commit` does not support such a branching strategy and has decided to not implement 146|an option, either on the [user's side](https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit/issues/2512) 147|or the [hook author's side](https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit/issues/2508), to define a branch for looking 148|up the latest available tag. 149| 150|Thus, `pre-commit autoupdate` is not usable for the hooks described here. 151| 152|You can avoid changing the `rev` to an unexpected value by using the `--repo` parameter (may be specified multiple 153|times), to explicitly list repositories that should be updated. An option to explicitly exclude 154|repositories [will not be implemented](https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit/issues/1959) into `pre-commit`. 155| 156|### Are there any alternatives to `pre-commit autoupdate`? 157| 158|You may use [pre-commit-update](https://pypi.org/project/pre-commit-update/) as an alternative to 159|`pre-commit autoupdate`. 160| 161|Since `pre-commit-update` can be used as a pre-commit hook itself, the easiest way 162|to make use of it would be to include it inside `.pre-commit-config.yaml`: 163| 164|```yaml 165|repos: 166|- repo: https://gitlab.com/vojko.pribudic.foss/pre-commit-update 167| rev: v0.5.1post1 168| hooks: 169| - id: pre-commit-update 170|- repo: https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry 171| rev: 1.8.3 172| hooks: 173| - id: poetry-check 174| - id: poetry-lock 175| - id: poetry-export 176| - id: poetry-install 177|``` 178| 179|Your `.pre-commit-config.yaml` repos will be checked and updated every time pre-commit hooks run. 180| 181|For more advanced configuration, please check the `pre-commit-update` documentation. --- END FILE: docs/pre-commit-hooks.md --- --- FILE: But if it's not, it will use 19|one that it has already created or create a brand new one for you. 20| 21|By default, Poetry will try to use the Python version used during Poetry's installation 22|to create the virtual environment for the current project. 23| 24|However, for various reasons, this Python version might not be compatible 25|with the `python` range supported by the project. In this case, Poetry will try 26|to find one that is and use it. If it's unable to do so then you will be prompted 27|to activate one explicitly, see [Switching environments](#switching-between-environments). 28| 29|{{% note %}} 30|If you use a tool like [pyenv](https://github.com/pyenv/pyenv) to manage different Python versions, 31|you can switch the current `python` of your shell and Poetry will use it to create 32|the new environment. 33| 34|For instance, if your project requires a newer Python than is available with 35|your system, a standard workflow would be: 36| 37|```bash 38|pyenv install 3.9.8 39|pyenv local 3.9.8 # Activate Python 3.9 for the current project 40|poetry install 41|``` 42| 43|{{% /note %}} 44| 45|{{% note %}} 46|Since version 1.2, Poetry no longer supports managing environments for Python 2.7. 47|{{% /note %}} 48| 49|## Switching between environments 50| 51|Sometimes this might not be feasible for your system, especially Windows where `pyenv` 52|is not available, or you simply prefer to have a more explicit control over your environment. 53|For this specific purpose, you can use the `env use` command to tell Poetry 54|which Python version to use for the current project. 55| 56|```bash 57|poetry env use /full/path/to/python 58|``` 59| 60|If you have the python executable in your `PATH` you can use it: 61| 62|```bash 63|poetry env use python3.7 64|``` 65| 66|You can even just use the minor Python version in this case: 67| 68|```bash 69|poetry env use 3.7 70|``` 71| 72|If you want to disable the explicitly activated virtual environment, you can use the 73|special `system` Python version to retrieve the default behavior: 74| 75|```bash 76|poetry env use system 77|``` 78| 79|## Activating the environment 80| 81|{{% note %}} 82|Looking for `poetry shell`? It was moved to a plugin: [`poetry-plugin-shell`](https://github.com/python-poetry/poetry-plugin-shell) 83|{{% /note %}} 84| 85|The `poetry env activate` command prints the activate command of the virtual environment to the console. 86|You can run the output command manually or feed it to the eval command of your shell to activate the environment. 87|This way you won't leave the current shell. 88| 89|{{< tabs tabTotal="3" tabID1="bash-csh-zsh" tabID2="fish" tabID3="powershell" tabName1="Bash/Zsh/Csh" tabName2="Fish" tabName3="Powershell" >}} 90| 91|{{< tab tabID="bash-csh-zsh" >}} 92| 93|```bash 94|$ eval $(poetry env activate) 95|(test-project-for-test) $ # Virtualenv entered 96|``` 97| 98|{{< /tab >}} 99|{{< tab tabID="fish" >}} 100| 101|```bash 102|$ eval (poetry env activate) 103|(test-project-for-test) $ # Virtualenv entered 104|``` 105| 106|{{< /tab >}} 107|{{< tab tabID="powershell" >}} 108| 109|```ps1 110|PS1> Invoke-Expression (poetry env activate) 111|(test-project-for-test) PS1> # Virtualenv entered 112|``` 113| 114|{{< /tab >}} 115|{{< /tabs >}} 116| 117|## Displaying the environment information 118| 119|If you want to get basic information about the currently activated virtual environment, 120|you can use the `env info` command: 121| 122|```bash 123|poetry env info 124|``` 125| 126|will output something similar to this: 127| 128|```text 129|Virtualenv 130|Python: 3.7.1 131|Implementation: CPython 132|Path: /path/to/poetry/cache/virtualenvs/test-O3eWbxRl-py3.7 133|Valid: True 134| 135|Base 136|Platform: darwin 137|OS: posix 138|Python: /path/to/main/python 139|``` 140| 141|If you only want to know the path to the virtual environment, you can pass the `--path` option 142|to `env info`: 143| 144|```bash 145|poetry env info --path 146|``` 147| 148|If you only want to know the path to the python executable (useful for running mypy from a global environment without installing it in the virtual environment), you can pass the `--executable` option 149|to `env info`: 150| 151|```bash 152|poetry env info --executable 153|``` 154| 155|## Listing the environments associated with the project 156| 157|You can also list all the virtual environments associated with the current project 158|with the `env list` command: 159| 160|```bash 161|poetry env list 162|``` 163| 164|will output something like the following: 165| 166|```text 167|test-O3eWbxRl-py3.6 168|test-O3eWbxRl-py3.7 (Activated) 169|``` 170| 171|You can pass the option `--full-path` to display the full path to the environments: 172| 173|```bash 174|poetry env list --full-path 175|``` 176| 177|## Deleting the environments 178| 179|Finally, you can delete existing virtual environments by using `env remove`: 180| 181|```bash 182|poetry env remove /full/path/to/python 183|poetry env remove python3.7 184|poetry env remove 3.7 185|poetry env remove test-O3eWbxRl-py3.7 186|``` 187| 188|You can delete more than one environment at a time. 189| 190|```bash 191|poetry env remove python3.6 python3.7 python3.8 192|``` 193| 194|Use the `--all` option to delete all virtual environments at once. 195| 196|```bash 197|poetry env remove --all 198|``` 199| 200|If you remove the currently activated virtual environment, it will be automatically deactivated. 201| 202|{{% note %}} 203|If you use the [`virtualenvs.in-project`]({{< relref "configuration#virtualenvsin-project" >}}) configuration, you 204|can simply use the command as shown below. 205| 206|```bash 207|poetry env remove 208|``` 209|{{% /note %}} --- END FILE:
